items.title: Coast Guard, Michigan State Police rescue missing hiker from Lake Superior island
items.author: PO3 Michael Lauofo
items.summary: CLEVELAND — The Coast Guard and Michigan State Police rescued an injured, ailing man Saturday after he went missing in Isle Royale National Park on Sept. 5.
items.body:
CLEVELAND — The Coast Guard and Michigan State Police rescued an injured, ailing man Saturday after he went missing in Isle Royale National Park on Sept. 5.

With the assistance of good Samaritan backpackers, Michigan State Police troopers and K-9 units located Craig Berg, 70, who was reportedly injured and hypothermic on Isle Royale.

An MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from Coast Guard Air Station Traverse City hoisted and transported him to Marquette Regional Airport in Gwinn, Michigan. Emergency medical services personnel staged at the airport transported Berg to a local hospital for further care.

On Friday, a 45-foot Response Boat-Medium crew from Coast Guard Station Portage and helicopter crew from Air Station Traverse City transported the troopers and K-9 units to Isle Royale to aid in search efforts.

“We’re thankful that missing hiker, Craig Berg, was found alive and alert on Isle Royale,” said Lt. Ben Eckola, Michigan State Police Eighth District PublicInformation Officer. “The collaboration and hard work of everyone involved in the search helped locate Craig safely. We appreciate the Michigan State Police personnel who helped, as well as our partners at the U.S. Coast Guard, National Park Service, Michigan Department of Natural Resources, Keweenaw County Sheriff’s Office, Wisconsin State Patrol, and Minnesota Department of Public Safety. We’re also thankful to the fellow hikers who helped, Isle Royale Seaplanes, and No One Left Behind K9 Search and Rescue. Everyone’s efforts played an important part in finding Craig.”

“This rescue is a testament to teamwork and what can be accomplished when first responders and members of the community come together,” said Senior Chief Petty Officer Wendy Janson, Command Duty Officer of Sector Northern Great Lakes command center. “We are extremely grateful we were able to get Mr. Berg safely off the island and deliver him tothe medical care he needed.”

Further details about Berg’s condition and the circumstances of his disappearance are still unknown.

items.title: Free rail travel expanded to bereaved veteran families this Remembrance weekend
items.summary: Bereaved military family members can travel for free on National Rail services to attend Remembrance events between 7 and 8 November 2026.
items.body:
hundreds of bereaved military family members will be able to travel by rail free of charge this Remembrance weekend across Britain

offer will help families attend Remembrance services and commemorative events, including the Cenotaph, without the cost of travel being a barrier

families have until 16 October 2026 to apply for free tickets, helping more bereaved relatives take part in the nation’s Remembrance

Hundreds of bereaved military family members will be able to travel by train free of charge this Remembrance weekend (7 to 8 November 2026), helping them attend memorial services and commemorative events to honour loved ones who died while serving in the Armed Forces.

For the first time, one next of kin of a service person who died while serving will be able to travel free of charge on National Rail services to attend Remembrance weekend events.

The move builds on the existing free travel offer for serving personnel and veterans, giving people breathing space and ensuring travel costs are not a barrier for families taking part in remembrance and reflection.

Eligible family members wishing to take up the offer have until 16 October to apply for a free ticket through the Defence Medical Welfare Service.

Rail Minister, Lord Hendy, said:

Remembrance weekend is a time for the nation to come together to honour those who made the ultimate sacrifice whilst serving our country. Bereaved families are at the heart of these commemorations and the cost of travel should not prevent them from being there to remember their loved ones. Extending free rail travel to next of kin will help more families attend Remembrance events, standing alongside communities, veterans and serving members of our Armed Forces as we honour and remember those who served.

Minister for Veterans and People, Calvin Bailey, said:

Remembrance is an opportunity for the nation to come together in recognition of the service and sacrifice of our Armed Forces. For bereaved families, this is a deeply personal time. We must never forget that behind every name we remember is a family whose lives have been changed forever. Providing free rail travel will help bereaved relatives come together and honour their loved one without financial barriers.

Remembrance is an opportunity for the nation to come together in recognition of the service and sacrifice of our Armed Forces. For bereaved families, this is a deeply personal time.

We must never forget that behind every name we remember is a family whose lives have been changed forever. Providing free rail travel will help bereaved relatives come together and honour their loved one without financial barriers.

Mikki Brett, the widow of the late Chief Petty Officer (CPO) Stuart Brett, who served in the Weapons Engineering branch of the Royal Navy and died in service in April 2023, spoke with Defence Minister Calvin Bailey this week.

Mikki Brett said:

It’s fantastic news that the in-service bereaved have been recognised for the support given to their loved ones with free train fares to remembrance events this year.

Mikki is already registered to come to the Cenotaph on Remembrance Sunday and will benefit directly from the new travel offer for those bereaved in service.

Ola Ogun, Co- CEO of Rail Delivery Group, said:

Railways have long been connected to remembrance commemorations, recognising the importance of their contribution during wartime. As an industry, we are proud to continue supporting this important national occasion by offering free travel to serving personnel and veterans. This year, we are especially pleased to extend that support to one next of kin of those who died while serving in the Armed Forces, recognising not only the sacrifice of those who served, but also the families who continue to carry their legacy and honour their memory.

This year, we are especially pleased to extend that support to one next of kin of those who died while serving in the Armed Forces, recognising not only the sacrifice of those who served, but also the families who continue to carry their legacy and honour their memory.

A spokesperson for SSAFA , the Armed Forces charity, said:

SSAFA welcomes the Department for Transport’s decision to extend free travel to bereaved military families during the Remembrance weekend. This change ensures that those who have lost loved ones in the service of their nation can travel to pay their respects without facing financial strain. It is a deeply meaningful gesture that properly honours the sacrifices of our Forces families, ensuring they can stand together with the nation in remembrance.

items.title: US Space Command Should Always Be Led by a Guardian
items.author: admin
items.summary: General Stephen Whiting took command of U.S. Space Command in January 2024, and if customary three-year tenures hold, his tour would end in January 2027. The question now before the President and Senate is who should follow him? Whoever they choose, it has to be a Guardian—and so should every successor thereafter. The post US Space Command Should Always Be Led by a Guardian appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

General Stephen Whiting took command of U.S. Space Command in January 2024, and if customary three-year tenures hold, his tour would end in January 2027. The question now before the President and Senate is who should follow him?

Whoever they choose, it has to be a Guardian—and so should every successor thereafter.

The reason is operational, not parochial: Guardians are the military professionals best prepared to integrate spacepower into global, multi-domain operations, and the Space Force exists to generate the nation’s combat-ready space forces.

Space is no longer an uncontested domain, merely enabling others; it is a warfighting domain and capable of delivering decisive effects. U.S. Space Command’s job is to secure space superiority to preserve access to space capabilities, and plan, execute, and integrate military spacepower into multi-domain global operations. Its commander therefore must be more than familiar with space-enabled capabilities. The position demands mastery of orbital warfare, space domain awareness, command and control, electromagnetic and cyber dependencies, counterspace threats, and the integration of space effects across every geographic combatant command. Guardians are the only service members who train from accession through senior command around that full mission set.

By law, the Space Force must provide freedom of operation for the United States in, from, and to space; conduct space operations; and protect U.S. interests in space. That statutory responsibility matters. Other services have space expertise to support their missions, but Congress made the Space Force uniquely responsible to organize, train, and equip forces for prompt and sustained space operations.

A Guardian commanding U.S. Space Command brings both the depth to fight for space superiority and the breadth to lead Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, Marines, and allied forces as a joint team. Jointness is not achieved by rotating a command among services for the sake of balance; it is achieved by selecting the officer best prepared to accomplish the assigned mission.

When U.S. Space Command was re-established in August 2019 , President Trump selected General John “Jay” Raymond , soon to be the first Space Force Guardian, as the commander. But this was a temporary one-year arrangement, as Gen. Raymond was also named the first Chief of Space Operations after the Space Force was created four months later. President Trump selected Army General James Dickinson to lead U.S. Space Command from August 2020 to January 2024. When Gen. Dickinson assumed command, the Space Force was still in its first year. No pool of seasoned Guardians existed to compete for the position.

That’s no longer the case. In 2023, President Biden nominated and the Senate confirmed Gen. Whiting for the position. Since then, the Space Force has continued to develop Guardian leaders with the critical operational experience, expertise, and an unparalleled understanding of space as a warfighting domain. Gen. Dickinson’s selection was a sound transitional exception, not a precedent for an enduring Army-Space Force rotation.

The Space Force now has multiple positions and pathways to prepare its senior leaders for the responsibilities of Commander, U.S. Space Command.

First is Combat Forces Command, which traces its lineage to Space Operations Command and Air Force Space Command, where Gen. Whiting and Gen. Raymond, respectively, commanded before taking the reins of U.S. Space Command. Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon is , the current commander of CFC. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. David “Rock” Miller , is still serving, now as Deputy Chief of Space Operations, Strategy, Plans, Programs and Requirements on the Space Force staff.

Second are the Space Force’s component commands, which present the service’s forces to different combatant commands. These component commanders range in rank from colonel to 3-star general in Lt. Gen. Dennis Bythewood at Space Forces-Space. These positions build essential experience in integrating space effects into combat operations and provide Guardians with a distinct expertise in integrating space effects with those of all domains to achieve national objectives terrestrially and in orbit. That pipeline now produces leaders who have both commanded space forces and integrated their effects across the U.S. military, the precise combination U.S. Space Command requires.

The Army’s June 2026 decision to create its own Space Operations Branch, along with U.S. Space Command’s relocation to Huntsville will understandably fuel an Army case to lead Space Command in the future. But neither development changes the underlying command requirement: to deliver space superiority in support of national objectives in all domains.

The Army branch is designed to improve Army component access to space-enabled capabilities at the tactical edge; it does not displace the Space Force’s responsibility for space warfare or its much broader mission set.

Likewise, while Redstone Arsenal’s Army space expertise will be valuable to U.S. Space Command, that expertise is both technical and geographical. It has little to do with governance. Locating a combatant command on an Army installation does not justify an Army claim to command it.

Some might argue that a Guardian commander would somehow make U.S. Space Command less joint. This is specious. The command will continue to employ capabilities and personnel from every service and work with the intelligence community, allies, and commercial partners. But to ensure space superiority, the officer heading U.S. Space Command must be able to make time-critical decisions to protect, defend, and employ space combat power under attack. At that level, the domain expertise inherent to Space Force Guardians is not a mere parochial preference; it is an operational warfighting requirement. Jointness does not require rotation for rotation’s sake. It requires the right commander for the mission.

The President should make the institutional logic explicit: future commanders of U.S. Space Command should come from the Space Force. The Senate should reinforce that standard in confirmation.

Doing so would align operational command with the service Congress created to protect U.S. interests in space. It would also sharpen accountability for space superiority and preserve, rather than diminish, the command’s joint character.

The move to Huntsville should deepen U.S. Space Command’s and the Space Force’s partnership with the Army, but should not blur responsibility for leading the nation’s space warfighting enterprise. Gen. Whiting’s successor should be a Guardian. So should every commander who follows.

items.title: Together in Purpose, United in Mission: Pacific Partnership 2026 Strengthens Multinational Cooperation
items.author: Courtesy

items.body:
KOTA KINABALU, Malaysia – From the shores of Dong Hoi, Vietnam, to the coast of Sibolga, Indonesia, across Dili, Timor-Leste, and now into Kota Kinabalu, Malaysia, Pacific Partnership 2026 (PP26) has brought together multinational military personnel from eight partner nations in support of the four lines of effort (LOE) during the humanitarian assistance and disaster management preparedness mission’s 20th anniversary in the Indo-Pacific, with each service member contributing a unique specialty or skill set toward a shared mission.

Over the duration of four mission stops, international armed forces service members from Australia, Canada, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Singapore, and the United Kingdom have integrated with U.S. forces and host nation partners, combining specialized expertise across the mission’s lines of effort and demonstrating how these capabilities become greater when brought together toward a common purpose.

For the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF), integration starts at the highest levels of the mission and expands into the communities the Pacific Partnership mission serves. For this year’s iteration, CAF Col. Alain Lafrenière is serving as deputy mission commander, making him the highest-ranking officer-in-charge (OIC) of partner-nation military members assigned to the mission and the first CAF service member to hold the position.

In addition, CAF Cmdr. Wendy Goulet is the mission’s multinational operations control commander (MNOCC), the second highest-ranking OIC of partner-nation military members assigned to the mission. For her roles and responsibilities as MNOCC, she oversees the planning, coordination, and execution of engagements involving partner nations in the mission.

“Throughout this deployment, I have learned that despite our cultural backgrounds and differences in how our militaries operate, we share many common values, goals, and challenges,” said Goulet. “I have also seen firsthand how even small engagements have a meaningful and lasting impact on the communities and nations we visit, making the work exceptionally rewarding.”

While Canada's contribution spans leadership, medical care, and host-nation outreach, Germany brings highly specialized dental expertise to PP26.

German Armed Forces dentists have conducted dental examinations and care during side-by-side medical exchanges with U.S. and host-nation medical personnel, sharing their professional knowledge while demonstrating how different military medical systems can work together to deliver care. Though small in number, their contributions have directly supported individual patient care throughout the duration of the mission.

“It is very interesting to experience how other nations serve their country in the same role as me, which I actually had not expected before,” said German Air Force Maj. Sarah Salomon, a dentist with PP26. “There are many parallels in structure and skills. Furthermore, the linguistic exchange in English is beneficial because I hardly ever have to use it at home. I am very pleased with the friendly cooperation between several nations.”

Australia's contribution to Pacific Partnership 2026 extended from the sea to the construction site, providing a capability rarely seen in a U.S. Navy-led mission: a partner nation's warship used as a platform, helping carry the mission from one stop to the next.

Royal Australian Navy (RAN) sailors, assigned to the amphibious Bay-class Landing Ship Dock (LSD) HMAS Choules (L100), welcomed and embarked PP26 personnel aboard the vessel while moored in Subic Bay, Philippines, in early July. Choules was critical in transporting the mission staff to and from one of the mission's five stops: Sibolga, Indonesia, in July, and a week-long administrative port visit to Singapore in August. Choules provided a crucial logistics function by easing the transportation of mission personnel and equipment between countries separated by thousands of miles of ocean.

“The biggest takeaway is the greater interoperability with partner nations, specifically USN [United States Navy] Seabees, ROKN [Republic of Korea Navy] engineers, and Malaysian Armed Forces,” said Australian Army Capt. Nicholas Filla, a civil engineer with PP26. “Improved networks and relationships with partner nations’ forces. Greater experience of contract administration and commanding deployed forces in a multinational, multicultural environment.”

Once ashore, RAN sailors and Australian Army engineers joined forces with U.S. Navy Seabees and host nation personnel on multiple construction projects, building tangible improvements for local communities. From carrying the mission forward at sea to building alongside partners on the ground, Australia's contribution demonstrated that multinational cooperation can strengthen every stage of PP26, from getting the team there to getting the job done.

Japan Self-Defense Forces and Singapore Armed Forces medical personnel supported numerous hours of training during several health engagements with host nation healthcare workers in the fields of emergency medicine, pharmacy, nursing, dentistry, and dive medicine. Japanese dentists and dental technicians worked side-by-side with German, Canadian, and U.S. counterparts to deliver multiple hours of oral hygiene care across Indonesia and Malaysia.

New Zealand and the Republic of Korea’s contributions have a broader approach, providing a multiservice team of disaster management specialists and civil engineering professionals and a medical contingent of nurses and surgeons respectively, focused on disaster response capabilities and construction projects.

Working with host-nation partners, the team shared knowledge and best practices for preparing for disasters before they occur. Together, the New Zealand and Republic of Korea teams demonstrate how even highly specialized capabilities can expand the reach and effectiveness of a multinational mission.

“This experience of service members from different countries working together as one team, transcending differences in language and working methods by sharing their expertise and experience,” said ROKN Cmdr. Yang Mi-Young, commanding officer of 1st NMCB of the 59th Mobile Construction Squadron. “This will become a great asset for future mission execution, strengthen the alliance’s credibility, and reinforce the multilateral cooperation framework.”

During the PP26 mission stop in Malaysia, mission personnel from all LOEs toured the British Royal Navy Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessel HMS Tamar (P233) while pierside in Kota Kinabalu. The tour included several damage control demonstrations where PP26 participants sharpened their hose handling and pipe patching skills alongside one another.

From medical exchanges and engineering projects to disaster preparedness and host nation outreach engagements, the impact of Pacific Partnership 2026 has been shaped by the partner nations who all came together to make each effort possible. Together, their collective capabilities demonstrate when nations unite around a common purpose, individual strengths become a greater force for partnership, preparedness and regional resilience.

Now in its 22nd iteration, the Pacific Partnership series is the largest annual multinational humanitarian assistance and disaster management preparedness mission conducted in the region. Pacific Partnership works collaboratively with host and partner nations to enhance regional interoperability and disaster response capabilities, increase security in the region, and foster new and enduring friendships in the Indo-Pacific.

items.title: Hawaii National Guard delivers emergency lifeline to Kauai patients following Storm Outages
items.author: SSG John Schoebel
items.summary: The Hawai‘i National Guard deployed a CH-47 Chinook helicopter to transport critical-care dialysis patients, caregivers and staff from Kaua‘i to O‘ahu on Sept. 10, 2026, following widespread power outages caused by Hurricane Lowell.
items.body:
LIHUE, Hawaii - The Hawai‘i National Guard deployed a CH-47 Chinook helicopter to transport critical-care dialysis patients, caregivers and staff from Kaua‘i to O‘ahu on Sept. 10, 2026, following widespread power outages caused by Hurricane Lowell.

Power disruptions left a local dialysis facility unable to operate, making it impossible to treat critical patients on island. While authorities initially planned to transport patients using commercial flights, reoccurring blackouts at the airport disabled Transportation Security Administration screening equipment. The delays inside and outside the terminal forced health officials to seek alternative transport options to prevent vulnerable patients from extended disruptions to their treatment.

Working directly with the Kaua‘i Emergency Management Agency, Chief Warrant Officer 2 Robin Eiland, an aviation liaison assigned to Bravo Company, 2nd Battalion, 211th Aviation Regiment, assisted a State of Hawai‘i Department of Health representative in submitting a formal request for assistance to mobilize military air assets.

Once approved, the Chinook flew the patients from Līhu‘e Airport directly to the Hawai‘i Army National Guard aviation hangar in Kalaeloa bypassing the airport congestion. Upon landing on O‘ahu, Honolulu Emergency Medical Services (EMS) personnel met the aircraft and transported the patients directly to local facilities for treatment.

“Dialysis is not something patients can simply postpone without serious consequences,” said Honolulu EMS Director Jim Ireland. “Our teams understand how critical these treatments are, and we are committed to doing everything we can to help ensure patients get the care they need. This response is a great example of multiple agencies working together to support our most vulnerable residents.”

The multi-agency life-safety mission moved from an idea to wheels-up execution very quickly, with the critical-care dialysis patients leaving Kaua‘i at 5:50 p.m. and leaving the airfield on Oahu in the EMS by 7:00 p.m..

"The mission went from a request to reality within hours," said Maj. Jerrod Avegalio, acting State Army Aviation Officer of the Hawaiʻi Army National Guard. "We were tracking the importance of the transport and that decisive action was needed. The combined efforts of our aviation maintenance to ensure ready aircraft, crews, flight operations, fuelers and every other ground support entity on both islands ultimately enabled us to respond safely and effectively when needed the most.”

Avegalio emphasized that Guard aviators and support staff remain on standby as recovery efforts continue across the island chain.

“I am extremely proud of what our team accomplished,” Avegalio added. “We will continue to stay ready to answer the call for our Kauaʻi ‘ohana during this difficult time.”

items.title: JBER remembers 25th Anniversary of 9/11
items.author: A1C Thomas Polk
items.summary: Exactly 25 years ago today, planes crashed into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. As Americans rallied together in the aftermath, they knew their lives would be forever changed. For the men and women of the U.S. Department of Defense, Sept. 11 also marked the start of a radical shift in the way the U.S. military continues to operate and defend the homeland. The emphasis became cultivating service members--including Airmen--who are ready to respond to any contingency, any time, anywhere in
items.body:
A day measured In years

Exactly 25 years ago today, planes crashed into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. As Americans rallied together in the aftermath, they knew their lives would be forever changed. For the men and women of the U.S. Department of Defense, Sept. 11 also marked the start of a radical shift in the way the U.S. military continues to operate and defend the homeland. The emphasis became cultivating service members--including Airmen--who are ready to respond to any contingency, any time, anywhere in the world.

“Now as we continue to evolve agile combat employment and multi-capable Airmen or mission ready Airmen, all of those things fall under the same need to be ready to respond,” said Chief Master Sgt. Edward Mueller, command chief for the 673d Air Base Wing, Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson.

A very different environment

For Airmen like Mueller, who was already in the service when 9/11 occurred, the military environment was a markedly different place. For example, security at military installations was more lenient, and federal regulations were not as robust. Oftentimes, U.S. citizens could drive into base through uncontrolled gates without showing an ID.

“Rolling through the gate at Mountain Home Air Force Base [in Idaho] before Sept. 11, when we used stickers on our car that showed that our vehicle and its passengers were authorized, security forces would either give you a nod or a wave to move you through the gate,” Mueller said.

Everything changed for Mueller and other service members on that fateful day. After the initial shock, orders were issued to mobilize the entire nation. Bases were on alert, personnel gearing up and leadership devising strategies in response. Personnel mobilized and deployed like never before. According to the https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2011/10/05/chapter-3-fighting-a-decade-long-war/, around 84% of active duty personnel deployed post 9/11, a 26% increase from pre-9/11 deployments.

This mobilization included even the newest members of the armed forces. For Chief Master Sgt. Kevin Helms, command chief for the Eleventh Air Force, Alaskan Command and NORAD Alaska Region, that was how his career started. He had just graduated high school and was about to enter basic training when he heard the news.

“I was staying with my brother-in-law, and I recall being awakened that morning, and it was right after the first aircraft had struck the towers,” he said.

Helms was resolute in his commitment to the nation, something he also noticed in his wingmen.

“It was a renewed focus from everybody that I went to basic training with,” he said. “That sense of purpose was immediately apparent.”

A shared mission

Urgency and focus were key in the following 9/11. Service members put their affairs in order and prepared to travel halfway across the world, often with nearly no notice.

“There were some of us newer Airmen who had [desert camouflage uniforms] with no stripes, no Air Force tapes, no name tapes,” said Mueller. “It was relatively quick for an operation of that size.”

Even with waves of deployments, newer members observed first-hand the capability and excellence of their brothers and sisters in arms. As a new Airmen at Little Rock AFB, Arkansas, Helms wanted to do what he could to join them.

“You're trying to do all your training, to get all your core tasks knocked out, that way you can get down there and contribute as fast as possible,” said Helms. “That was my focus: ‘How can I upgrade, and how can I be ready to go whenever that next deployment goes out?’”

As new installations were established in the Middle East, personnel began to operate in the theater to ensure successful missions. Timelines were constantly in flux as the U.S. military responded to new information, and service members didn’t always know how long they’d be away from family--or how soon they’d have to leave again.

“For most of us, it was deployments for about six months,” said Chief Master Sgt. Jason Parrish, senior enlisted leader of the 673rd Mission Support Group. “You'd come home for four to six months, and then you would deploy again, especially in some of our high-demand career fields like security forces.”

Building a new type of resiliency

For the next several years, the U.S. was ever vigilant and proactive in its actions to defend the country and reduce threats to security. The National Guard engaged more actively in overseas deployments. Military branches accelerated technological developments, creating enhanced intelligence and combat systems. There was also an increased support for the DOD and its members. Patriotism welled up across the states, resulting in an 8% increase in enlistments . The DOD’s response following 9/11 had each branch engaged together, reinforcing their joint interoperability and camaraderie.

“I saw probably the height of togetherness that I can remember in my lifetime,” said Mueller. “No matter what the differences were in our country, political or social, coming out of the 1990s, it was a terrible tragedy, but it was one that unified the nation.”

For many service members, that one day shaped the rest of their career. From training to deployments and objectives, the attacks set the tone for the future of the DOD. Those who served during 9/11 have guided and evolved the armed forces into what they are today, carrying on a now 250-year-old legacy of liberty and justice.

Now with decades of information and experience, the U.S. and the Department of War have improved and reinvisioned national security, strengthening defense and deterring adversaries. More than ever, the armed forces are making great efforts to sustain and improve operability, power projection and agile combat employment to meet any challenge. The men and women who serve have been leading the way, be it 250 years or 25 years, and will continue to do so for the safety and prosperity of the nation.

“I've seen our military change, where our focus on readiness really emerged from Sept. 11, and has continued to evolve over the last 29 years,” said Parrish. “As combat continues to evolve over time, so do our expectations and our need from our ‘capital A’ Airmen, and I absolutely believe that the best and brightest members of our nation, less than 1% of our nation's citizens of any generation, serve in this uniform.”

items.title: NAVFAC Pacific Hosts Specialized Job Fair to Recruit Engineering Talent
items.author: Corwin Colbert
items.summary: JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii – Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Pacific hosted a successful job fair Sept. 10 at the Ala Moana Hotel in Honolulu, Hawaii in an effort to recruit and hire permanent, full-time civilian positions across the Pacific area of operations.
items.body:
JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM , Hawaii – Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Pacific hosted a successful job fair Sept. 10 at the Ala Moana Hotel in Honolulu, Hawaii in an effort to recruit and hire permanent, full-time civilian positions across the Pacific area of operations.

"Investing directly in our people is vital to meeting our mission requirements,” said NAVFAC Pacific Vice Commander Capt. Brent Paul. “Tapping into our local talent pool to recruit a highly skilled workforce empowers our team by providing the operational foundation needed to build, maintain, and defend our posture across the Pacific theater.”

Human Resources representatives from NAVFAC Pacific, NAVFAC Hawaii, NAVFAC Engineering and Expeditionary Warfare Center and the Office of Civilian Human Resources within the Department of the Navy were in attendance recruiting a variety of professional disciplines, to include: engineers, construction managers, program and project managers, architects, engineering technicians and contract specialists.

“The scale of our current projects in Pearl Harbor and Washington State represents a generational investment in national security infrastructure,” said NAVFAC Pacific Chief Engineer Marc Wong. “To deliver on these critical missions, NAVFAC Pacific is seeking top-tier acquisition, facilities, and engineering talent ready to tackle some of the largest, most complex engineering challenges in the nation.”

The event drew nearly 300 in-person applicants and yielded dozens of onsite interviews, culminating in NAVFAC extending 30 tentative on-the-spot job offers to highly qualified candidates, with follow-on hiring actions planned in the coming weeks for many of the other applications received.

“I am incredibly proud of our team for executing such an outstanding event," said Wong. "Seeing so many driven individuals eager to contribute to our landmark projects proves that we are actively recruiting the very talent that will shape our nation's readiness for decades to come.”

The mission of NAVFAC Pacific is we plan, design, build and deliver resilient facilities infrastructure, expertly delivering construction, engineering and contracting services to our supported commanders.

items.title: Coast Guard rescues 2 from vessel fire on Lake Michigan
items.author: PO3 Michael Lauofo
items.summary: CLEVELAND— The Coast Guard responded to a report of a vessel fire with two people aboard near the entrance of the Grand Haven Channel on Lake Michigan Friday.
items.body:
Story by Petty Officer 3rd Class Michael Lauofo

U.S. Coast Guard Great Lakes

CLEVELAND— The Coast Guard responded to a report of a vessel fire with two people aboard near the entrance of the Grand Haven Channel on Lake Michigan Friday.

Coast Guard Sector Lake Michigan watchstanders received notification from Ottawa County Dispatch at 3:27 p.m. of a 30-foot pleasure craft reported as smoking and disabled.

Watchstanders directed the launch of a Coast Guard Station Grand Haven 45-foot Response Boat-Medium crew and issued an urgent marine information broadcast.

The station crew arrived on scene and transferred both individuals to the RB-M. The crew placed the vessel in tow, controlling the fire during transit by using a pump and fire extinguisher.

The boat crew towed the vessel and its passengers safely back to North Shore Marina in the Grand River with no pollution reported.

For more information, please contact Great Lakes District Public Affairs at 216-902-6020, or via email at GLDPublicAffairs@uscg.mil.

items.title: Indo-Pacific military leaders gather for 2026 U.S. Naval War College Flag-Level course in Hawaii
items.author: PO2 Connor Burns
items.summary: Senior military leaders from 19 Indo-Pacific nations came together to explore combined maritime command-and-control concepts and mechanisms as the U.S. Naval War College's (NWC) College of Maritime Operational Warfare completed its Combined Force Maritime Component Commander (CFMCC) flag course in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, Aug. 27 to Sept. 2.
items.body:
Senior military leaders from 19 Indo-Pacific nations came together to explore combined maritime command-and-control concepts and mechanisms as the U.S. Naval War College's (NWC) College of Maritime Operational Warfare completed its Combined Force Maritime Component Commander (CFMCC) flag course in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, Aug. 27 to Sept. 2.

CFMCC is designed to give senior leaders from all military services and partner nations a broad perspective of the operational level of war and to prepare them for regional leadership.

Speakers at this iteration of the course included U.S. Navy Adm. Steve Koehler, commander, U.S. Pacific Fleet; former Chief of Naval Staff of the Indian Navy and current NWC Chief of Naval Operations Distinguished Fellow Nirmal K. Verma; Gen. Ronald P. Clark, commander, U.S. Army Pacific, and numerous representatives and scholars from NWC, the U.S. Air Force, Army, Coast Guard, Marine Corps, Department of War and other organizations.

"This course brought together so many top officers from across the Pacific and beyond,” said U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Darryl Walker, NWC President. “It truly serves to highlight the role the U.S. Naval War College plays in forging unbreakable bonds between partners and allies across great distances. Perhaps more importantly, CFMCC provides our joint and combined military leaders a shared awareness of the operational level of war, ensuring that our warfighters can be employed as a united force in the pursuit of common goals, built on a common understanding of the battle space. The value of this course cannot be overstated."

A one-week course, CFMCC is taught at the headquarters of a U.S. Navy regional fleet multiple times each year. CFMCC graduates gain the ability to effectively communicate and advance the understanding of security issues between participating nations.

“Success in the maritime domain depends on our ability to operate together as a cohesive force. CFMCC provides leaders the opportunity to strengthen trust, sharpen our understanding of joint and combined operations, and grow the relationships that enable us to respond decisively to shared challenges,” said Koehler. “By investing in these relationships today, we build the combined capability and confidence needed to meet tomorrow’s challenges.”

Established in 1884, NWC informs today’s decision-makers and educates tomorrow’s leaders by providing educational experiences and learning opportunities that develop their ability to hedge aggressively, innovate continuously, fight distributively, delegate confidently, and command with clarity within complex battlespaces.

items.title: NETCOM honors lives lost, service and sacrifice during 25th anniversary Sept. 11 remembrance ceremony
items.author: Gabriel Archer
items.summary: Soldiers, civilians, families and guests gathered at the Greely Hall flagpole Sept. 11 for a remembrance ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.
items.body: FORT HUACHUCA, AZ— Soldiers, civilians, families and guests gathered at the Greely Hall flagpole Sept. 11 for a remembrance ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. Hosted by the U.S. Army Network Enterprise Technology Command (NETCOM) Command Chaplain Section, the ceremony honored the nearly 3,000 people killed in New York, at the Pentagon and near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. It also recognized the first responders, service members, veterans and families whose lives were changed by the attacks and the conflicts that followed. “Twenty-five years ago today, on September 11, 2001, our nation experienced an attack that changed the course of American history,” said Sgt. 1st Class William Rogers, narrator for the ceremony and a member of the NETCOM Command Chaplain Section. “For some gathered here, the images, sounds and emotions of that morning remain vivid,” Rogers said. “For others, September 11th is a history learned from parents, teachers, leaders and those who served before them.” The observance began with an invocation from Maj. Tony Hunley, NETCOM deputy command chaplain, followed by the national anthem. Command Sgt. Maj. Adam Schuessler, NETCOM command sergeant major, provided senior leader remarks. The ceremony recounted the events of that morning, including the attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, as well as the actions of passengers and crew members aboard United Airlines Flight 93 who resisted the hijackers and prevented the aircraft from reaching its intended target. Organizers used four symbols to represent the places, people and generations connected to the attacks and their aftermath. Assistant Chief Zachary Sielaff of the Fort Huachuca Fire Department placed a firefighter’s helmet in remembrance of the first responders who ran toward danger while others sought safety. Robert Story, who was serving the nation in uniform on Sept. 11, 2001, placed a folded American flag to honor those killed at the Pentagon and represent the resolve of a nation wounded by the attack. Pfc. Nilah Masdeu, a Soldier born after Sept. 11, 2001, placed a single white rose in memory of the passengers and crew members of Flight 93. Her participation represented a generation that did not witness the attacks but has inherited the responsibility to remember their lessons. Sgt. Maj. Adrian Say, a veteran of the conflicts that followed Sept. 11, placed a pair of combat boots in honor of the service members who answered the nation’s call and the families who supported them. “A helmet, a flag, a rose, a pair of boots. Different symbols, one story,” Rogers said during the ceremony. “A nation attacked, a people who responded and a promise that, 25 years later: We still remember.” The ceremony concluded with a moment of silence for the victims of Sept. 11 and all those whose lives were forever changed by the attacks. Emergency sirens sounded during the observance, followed by the playing of taps. “Today, we gather as one community, not simply to remember how our nation was attacked, but to remember the people we lost, those who answered the call and the responsibility entrusted to the generations who followed,” Rogers said. The event concluded with an invitation for attendees to gather for refreshments in the Greely Hall foyer.

items.title: At Pentagon, Trump Leads 9/11 Commemoration on 25th Anniversary
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: President Donald Trump and government and military leaders past and present paid tribute to the victims, survivors, and heroes of the Sept. 11 terrorist attack on the Pentagon, marking 25 years since a hijacked plane flew into the building, killing... The post At Pentagon, Trump Leads 9/11 Commemoration on 25th Anniversary appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

President Donald Trump and government and military leaders past and present paid tribute to the victims, survivors, and heroes of the Sept. 11 terrorist attack on the Pentagon, marking 25 years since a hijacked plane flew into the building, killing 184 victims.

As rain poured down and the sun rose in the east, a massive American flag was unfurled atop the Pentagon wall, its stars and stripes flooding down the concrete facade, reenacting what first responders did on Sept. 12, 2001—and as they have done on every 9/11 anniversary since.

Hours later, Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice took turns at the lectern, each vowing to “never forget” the 2,977 American lives that day in New York, Washington, and Shanksville, Pa. In a coordinated attack, four U.S. airliners were hijacked that day. The first two struck the twin World Trade Center towers in New York City, the third slammed into the Pentagon, and the fourth, brought down after passengers stormed the cockpit, crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.

“A Navy airman had just gotten off the phone with his 10-year-old son,” Trump said. “A secretary was celebrating her 46th birthday. … A sergeant major was chatting with some colleagues he had hosted for a dinner party over the weekend. At 9:37 a.m., every single one of those people and every person at that sergeant major’s party was murdered by terrorists who flew Flight 77 straight into this legendary building.”

Rice, who was President Bush’s National Security Advisory in 2001, recounted her experience on 9/11 , “the horror and the shock that I felt” as a TV in the White House bunker displayed images of smoke rising from the Pentagon.

Yet in the midst of disaster, she added, military personnel and civilians alike responded with courage. “It is fitting that here at the Pentagon, we reflect not just on what happened here, but what in that moment of crisis, people did here,” she said. “They summoned a will and a spirit, a sense of obligation that our military lives by every day—I will stand between danger and my fellow citizens, I will leave no comrade behind, I will go, I will serve, I will do my duty.”

Caine, who as a young major scrambled in an F-16 to protect Washington D.C. on 9/11, called the anniversary not just a “story of loss” but one of “great American courage, selfless service, and those who’ve made the choice to carry those memories forward.”

More than 40 federal, state, and local agencies responded to the attack on the Pentagon. Rice described how then-Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld pulled people to safety “as his security detail begged him to flee the danger.” Trump described how, on Sept. 12, Army Maj. Gen. James Jackson ordered the American flag to be hung from the side of the Pentagon.

“First responders climbed to top the walls and hung it next to the gaping holes in this building as a symbol of American defiance,” Trump said. “This morning, that same flag is here to my right for the first time since 2001, along with three firefighters who raised it, Joseph Morabito, Scott Morgan, and Carl Solberg.”

Hegseth, who joined the U.S. Army in the years after 9/11, said the attacks “inspired millions to step forward instead and say, ‘send me.’” Now, 25 years later, he acknowledged that many service members “do not remember 9/11; many were not even born yet. And that leaves it to us on this day and others like it to pass down that memory to our kids, to my kids, to yours, to my grandkids, to yours.”

Both Trump and Hegseth made reference to the ongoing conflict with Iran, calling the Iranian government “the world’s number one sponsor of terror” and connecting the response to 9/11 to the ongoing hostilities.

For the most part, though, leaders focused their remarks on the lives lost in the attacks, the bravery of the survivors and first responders, and the national unity forged in the response.

“September 11th reminded us of the terrible power of hate,” Trump said. “The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail and to win.”

items.title: Fort Buchanan marks 25th anniversary of 9/11, passes legacy of remembrance to new generation
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Elected officials, service members, Department of the Army civilians, families, students and community members gathered at Antilles High School on Sept. 11 to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks and help ensure a new generation understands and remembers the events that changed the nation.
items.body: FORT BUCHANAN, Puerto Rico — Elected officials, service members, Department of the Army civilians, families, students and community members gathered at Antilles High School on Sept. 11 to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks and help ensure a new generation understands and remembers the events that changed the nation. The Fort Buchanan Fire Department led the remembrance ceremony, joined by firefighters and first responders from surrounding Puerto Rico communities. Their participation honored the firefighters, police officers, emergency personnel and civilians who responded to the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, while highlighting the partnerships that connect the installation with the communities beyond its gates. Niels Mateo, Antilles High School principal and retired Navy veteran, delivered the keynote address. Twenty-five years earlier, Mateo was a Navy officer serving at the Pentagon when terrorists attacked the building. “For me, September 11 is not simply a chapter in a history book,” Mateo told the audience. “It is a day I lived.” Speaking before students who were born years after the attacks, Mateo emphasized the responsibility of those who remember 9/11 to share its lessons with generations that did not experience it. “Because when living memory begins to fade, remembrance becomes a responsibility,” Mateo said. Mateo also connected Puerto Rico directly to the national response that followed the attacks. Puerto Rican service members were among the thousands who mobilized, deployed and supported military operations in the years that followed. “Puerto Rico did not watch history from the sidelines,” Mateo said. “Puerto Rico answered the call.” The ceremony brought together the military and civilian communities to remember nearly 3,000 people killed in the attacks and recognize the service and sacrifice of those who responded at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. For Fort Buchanan, the commemoration also provided an opportunity to connect students with the experiences of those who witnessed the attacks and served during the years that followed. “‘Never Forget’ must be more than a phrase,” Mateo said. “It must be a promise.” Mateo closed by challenging the audience to carry that promise forward. “Buildings can be rebuilt. Institutions can recover. A nation can heal — but only if its people remember what was lost, honor those who served, and remain united around the principles they are determined to defend.” Twenty-five years after 9/11, the gathering demonstrated that remembrance extends beyond those who witnessed the attacks. Through education, community partnership and shared remembrance, Fort Buchanan continues helping pass their stories and lessons to the generations that will carry them forward.

items.title: Puerto Rico Senate recognizes Fort Buchanan’s readiness role during 9/11 remembrance
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Service members and Department of the Army civilians from Fort Buchanan joined elected officials, federal and state law enforcement representatives and community members at the Puerto Rico Capitol on Sept. 11 to honor those killed in the 2001 terrorist attacks, commemorate the 25th anniversary of 9/11 and highlight the enduring partnership between Puerto Rico’s communities and the military.
items.body:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — Service members and Department of the Army civilians from Fort Buchanan joined elected officials, federal and state law enforcement representatives and community members at the Puerto Rico Capitol on Sept. 11 to honor those killed in the 2001 terrorist attacks, commemorate the 25th anniversary of 9/11 and highlight the enduring partnership between Puerto Rico’s communities and the military.

The Puerto Rico Senate hosted the remembrance ceremony in the Capitol Rotunda, where Ulises Marrero, Fort Buchanan acting garrison manager, represented the Army community on the island.

“From the headquarters of the U.S. Army in the Caribbean, our installation has supported for decades the readiness, mobilization and deployment of the forces our nation needs,” Marrero said. “After Sept. 11, that mission took on an even greater significance.”

During the ceremony, Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz presented Marrero with an official recognition of Fort Buchanan’s role as a readiness-enabling platform that supported military units training and mobilizing following the attacks.

The recognition, and the participation of military, government, law enforcement and community representatives in the ceremony, reflected the growing connection between Fort Buchanan and the community it serves. That relationship has expanded beyond installation boundaries through increased collaboration with local and federal government agencies, municipalities and community organizations.

Rivera Schatz reflected on the continuing human impact of the attacks.

“There are still empty chairs at the table, birthdays that were never celebrated, children who grew up without their fathers or mothers,” Rivera Schatz said. “And although time eases the pain, it certainly does not erase it, nor should it.”

He also emphasized Puerto Rico’s role in protecting the nation, describing the island as a U.S. “gateway and frontier” and recognizing the contributions of military, federal, state and emergency response organizations.

“Sept. 11 did not end that morning,” Rivera Schatz said. “The mission of protecting this nation continues every day, and it continues here in Puerto Rico.”

Twenty-five years after the attacks, Fort Buchanan continues serving as the Army’s home in the Caribbean, supporting training, logistics, sustainment and mobilization while strengthening relationships with the communities and institutions surrounding the installation.

“May this day remind us that freedom requires commitment, security requires vigilance, and national unity is our greatest strength,” Marrero said. “From Fort Buchanan, we reaffirm our commitment to continue working alongside government, our communities and our armed forces to keep our nation prepared and secure.”

Fort Buchanan supports approximately 15,000 military personnel, including active-duty Soldiers, Army Reserve, Puerto Rico National Guard, Marine Corps Reserve and Navy Reserve members. The installation’s mission is to enable readiness and facilitate the deployment of forces anytime, anywhere. Partnerships with neighboring communities enhance the installation’s ability to sustain its mission while contributing to the resilience of those communities.

items.title: 1st MLG inspector general team awarded for superior performance
items.author: LCpl Katherine Fohn
items.summary: MARINE CORPS BASE CAMP PENDLETON, Calif. -- The inspector general team of 1st Marine Logistics Group received the General Shoup Superior Unit Performance Award at the Inspector General of the Marine Corps training symposium in Quantico, Virginia, Aug. 25-28, 2026.
items.body: MARINE CORPS BASE CAMP PENDLETON, Calif. -- The inspector general team of 1st Marine Logistics Group received the General Shoup Superior Unit Performance Award at the Inspector General of the Marine Corps training symposium in Quantico, Virginia, Aug. 25-28, 2026. The award is presented to the inspector general’s office that upholds the highest level of efficiency, integrity and mission readiness following an inspection by the Inspector General of the Marine Corps that assessed different functional areas within 1st MLG. The responsibilities of U.S. Marine Corps Lt. Col. Duong Dam, command inspector general, and Mr. Thomas Gresser, deputy inspector general, both with 1st MLG, include ensuring command readiness by inspecting functional areas, such as efficiency and readiness programs, welfare programs, operations, safety, institutional integrity and oversight, as well as personnel preservation. Additionally, the inspector general’s office ensures that commands within the unit are adhering to orders and regulations. “We’re here to assist the Marines in any way possible to ensure that they’re meeting fundamental readiness,” said Gresser. A large part of their work relies on building relationships with commands and ensuring that they have continuous communication. They serve as an unbiased office where Marines can go to get advice, address issues and ensure that they have the right resources to resolve issues they may be experiencing. Dam said staying neutral is a key point to having an office where Marines can come in and voice their concerns so that they can point them in the right direction. To hold a high standard, Gresser said that they largely rely on teamwork, and not only that the teamwork that occurs within their office, but also working alongside commanders with different missions. Having continuous communication and building trust with each command contributed to the MLG upholding the standards in each functional area. The award was a recognition of everyone’s hard work that happens behind the scenes that typically isn’t seen at all command levels, said Gresser. At the training symposium where they were presented with the award, units were able to provide their best practices and gain a better understanding about how the IGMC is bringing change to the Marine Corps as an organization. As for the next inspection, they said that they want to do better. Although commands are continuously changing, the inspector general’s team goal is to continue maintaining the highest standard of efficiency, integrity and readiness that they have set for 1st MLG. “I believe in continuous improvement,” said Dam. “Marines should leave any place better than he or she found it.”

items.title: Team Orlando military and civilian personnel observe 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: More than 200 Soldiers, Sailors, Marines, government civilian employees and industry partners who help make up Team Orlando gathered at Warfighter Park on board Naval Support Activity Orlando on Sept. 11, 2026, for a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks on the United States.
items.body:
More than 200 Soldiers, Sailors, Marines, government civilian employees and industry partners who help make up Team Orlando gathered at Warfighter Park on board Naval Support Activity Orlando on Sept. 11, 2026, for a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks on the United States.

The staff of the U.S. Army’s Capability Program Executive Simulation, Training, Test and Threat (CPE ST3) sponsored the ceremony with a theme of “Remembrance, resilience, and service,” with Brig. Gen. Christine A. Beeler, capability program executive for CPE ST3, serving as the keynote speaker.

“Remembrance is more than recalling events, it is carrying forward the truth, honoring those we lost, and ensuring future generations understand the significance of that day,” Beeler told the audience during her remarks. “For the United States Army, Sept. 11 reshaped a generation. It changed our profession, accelerated innovation, and called forth service from Soldiers, families, and communities who sustained the mission for years.”

Beeler thanked the CPE ST3 staff and other members of Team Orlando for their work in simulation, training, test, and threat capabilities, and their tireless efforts to help improve the readiness of the Joint Force and train America’s warfighters.

“As we mark 25 years, remembrance has evolved; in 2001, it was shock, grief, and rescue. In the years that followed, it became deployment, sacrifice, and endurance,” Beeler said. “Today, remembrance is a duty - to teach, honor, and connect memory to mission. “We Will Never Forget” must be something we live through service, decisions, and care for one another.

Following Beeler’s remarks, a wreath was placed in honor of the 2,753 lives lost in New York, 184 lives lost at the Pentagon, and 40 lives lost in Pennsylvania.

Individuals taking part in the wreath ceremony were Department of the Navy police officer Steve Delrosario, representing the first responders called into action that day, and Army Capt. Cristian Acosta, assigned to Project Manager Simulation staff at CPE ST3, representing the U.S. military who responded with the War on Terror around the world.

Delrosario, who was in middle school on 9/11, said he joined the U.S. Air Force after graduating high school to serve his country. Acosta, who was four years old at the time, grew up in a world shaped by the events of that day.

“I was inspired by the courage and selfless sacrifice of an entire generation that answered the call to defend our freedom,” Acosta said. “That enduring legacy defined my sense of duty, making the decision to serve in the United States Army a personal commitment to protect our nation and its values.”

Following the presentation of the wreath, a brief timeline of the events that took place on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, was read aloud. The sound of a ceremonial bell marked the time of the impact of the four plane crashes as well as the collapse of both the South and North towers of the World Trade Center in New York.

A moment of silence followed, along with the playing of Taps to honor the 2,977 lives lost on 9/11. Following the conclusion of the ceremony, those who attended were invited to view the wreath and pay their respects to the fallen.

The immediate response and evolution of Army capabilities in the aftermath of 9/11 forged a generation of adaptive leaders and modern warfighters who form the foundation of today’s Joint Force.

Today, the Army serves as the foundation of that Joint Force, providing the foundational capabilities – from logistics and engineering to intelligence and maneuver forces – that enable all other branches to project power globally.

Headquartered in Orlando, Florida, CPE ST3 is comprised of a highly skilled and diverse workforce of 980 Soldiers, Army civilians and contractors, who work with Army partners to enhance operational readiness and support the Army’s modernization efforts by fielding and sustaining the next generation of multi-domain operations testing, training and information operations capabilities.

items.title: Air Force Tests Ground Stations for Commanding CCAs, Eyes Contract Next Summer
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Air Force announced Aug. 13 it recently tested prototypes for a portable ground station for commanding and controlling semi-autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft, and a spokesperson now says the plan is to award a contract for the effort next summer. The post Air Force Tests Ground Stations for Commanding CCAs, Eyes Contract Next Summer appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

Editor’s Note: This article was updated Sept. 11 to include information from the 178th Wing and the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center.

The Air Force announced Aug. 13 it recently tested prototypes for a portable ground station for commanding and controlling semi-autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft , and a spokesperson now says the plan is to award a contract for the effort next summer.

The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Agile Development Office revealed the progress on the Portable Command and Control Enclave, or C2E, in a release explaining how it evaluated the prototypes at Springfield Air National Guard Base, Ohio.

A combined team from the Experimental Operations Unit, Air Combat Command, and the AFLCMC’s Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch tested various metrics, such as weight, time to power on, time to connect, time to command, and size packed on a pallet.

“We cannot give specific examples due to the ongoing evaluation; however, broadly, feedback was provided to improve upon on how the equipment was packed, setup configurations, and connectivity,” an Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The EOU also gave feedback on how they intend to use the applications in the field.”

“The next phase focusing on cloud testing will run through the spring,” the spokesperson added. “The C2E program includes multiple form factors, and the plan is to award an initial integration partner in the early summer.”

Five unnamed companies participated in the C2E “fly-off” at Springfield. The spokesperson declined to identify the companies, citing operational security concerns.

CCAs are semi-autonomous drones the Air Force is pursuing to bolster its combat “mass” at a lower cost than manned fighters. The first iteration of CCAs, to be built by General Atomics Aeronautical Systems and Anduril Industries, will focus on air-to-air missions, but future versions could carry out missions such as air-to-ground strikes, reconnaissance, or electronic warfare operations.

The CCA concept has long been for these drones to fly alongside crewed aircraft as “wingmen” and take directions from human pilots. But Air Force officials have discussed the potential for controlling them from other locations.

The Ohio flyoff used the AFRL SkyVision system, a ground-based “detect-and-avoid” system that lets air traffic controllers use radar feeds to follow Group 1-5 drones Beyond Line of Sight across more than 200 square miles of airspace without a chase aircraft.

While the C2 enclave has been tested in a lab, this was the first physical fly-off using multiple prototypes in a real-world setting.

And, of course, it rained.

“Rainy weather conditions added novel considerations for testing that we wouldn’t have otherwise experienced in a controlled environment,” the Air Force spokesperson said.

Beyond the weather, the team learned more about “the logistics of moving equipment outside of usual indoor facilities, like reducing gear weight and optimizing equipment setup,” the spokesperson added.

Airmen from the 178th provided the space and helped with setup and coordination of the enclave testing.

The wing has worked with the SkyVision system for this and other testing needs since it went operational in 2019. Just last year the unit flew an MQ-9A in this airspace as part of a counter-UAS experiment with the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Ohio Department of Transportation UAS Center, spokeswoman Maj. Courtney Slater told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

More Control Options

Col. Timothy Helfrich, the service’s portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, first mentioned the C2E program in June, and a spokesperson subsequently described the idea as separate from the software fighter pilots will use to control CCAs and instead called it “an application suite on a range of networks to enable the right operator, with the right permissions, to operate CCA.”

Beyond fighter pilots, CCAs could be controlled from battle management aircraft like the E-7 Wedgetail. But the portable C2E effort is focused on the ground. The prototypes being evaluated are command-and-control systems meant to be rapidly deployed and operated anywhere worldwide, even in austere environments, the Air Force’s Aug. 13 release said.

After testing the command-and-control systems’ mobility and footprints, the Air Force said vendors carried out another round of demonstrations to show how well their software operated.

The Air Force said these evaluations mark “a pivotal milestone in advancing the tactical control of semi-autonomous systems” and are a critical first step towards selecting a vendor to integrate a C2E system.

While the release did not specify which contractors participated in the evaluations, Anduril has already touted its own system, Menace-T, as capable of controlling its YFQ-44A Collaborative Combat Aircraft. In April, the firm said it used Menace-T—which consists of two portable cases and a rugged laptop—to upload mission plans, initiate autonomous taxi and takeoff, task the aircraft while in flight, and manage post-flight data ingestion and checks.

The information collected from the Air Force’s Ohio demonstrations will help speed up the acquisition strategy for C2E and help shape the selection process going forward. A second C2E prototype phase will soon begin, the Air Force said, and vendors are expected to further refine and demonstrate their systems’ cloud capabilities.

Once the Air Force selects a C2E system, the service said, it will go to the Experimental Operations Unit, which is currently testing CCAs, to support agile combat employment operations. The C2E system will directly control production CCAs, the Air Force said, “ensuring service members maintain a decisive advantage in contested environments.”

“Getting prototypes into the hands of our operational and acquisitions warfighters for a swift, combined evaluation is a direct embodiment of acquisition transformation,” Agile Development Office director Col. Eric Reagan said. “This partnership allows us to accelerate the fielding of the best-value capabilities to the Department of War,” using the alternative name for the Defense Department.

items.title: Pentagon looks to AI to identify space and missile threats
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: The Pentagon is seeking artificial intelligence that can cut through the confusion of missile defense.
items.body:
Pentagon

Pentagon looks to AI to identify space and missile threats

A ground-based interceptor missile launches during a test in California in 2021. (Airman Kadielle Shaw/U.S. Space Force)

Missile defense in wartime involves many complications. Human operators must deal with high-speed objects, short timelines and sensor data that isn’t always clear.

The Pentagon now wants artificial intelligence that can cut through the confusion.

It’s seeking “AI-based software tools to turn fragmented sensor data into a continuously updated understanding of space and missile threats fast enough to drive operational decisions,” according to the Defense Innovation Unit solicitation , which is due Sept. 24. “Existing tools struggle to distinguish closely spaced objects, track emerging threats, and keep threat models current.”

The project, known as the “Space Threat Intelligence Synthesis Engine,” will leverage AI’s greatest strength: the ability to quickly analyze reams of data. The software will fuse “massive streams of multi-source data, including live video, satellite imagery, radar and sensor feeds, geospatial data, and classified intelligence reports.”

“By automating advanced cross-data correlation, the architecture aims to uncover hidden patterns, complex operational relationships, and predictive threat behaviors far beyond the capabilities of human analysis alone.”

Ultimately, the system should “generate actionable, confidence-scored alerts supporting analyst-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop, or automated workflows.”

The AI will help human operators — and other machines.

It will provide “intuitive, human-readable visualizations for frontline operators and low-latency, machine-to-machine APIs to drive automated command-and-control (C2) workflows.”

DIU is aiming for an open-source system with a latency delay of no more than five seconds — and preferably no more than two seconds — between the arrival of data and the results being displayed. Throughput should be 20 to 30 megabytes per minute, with bursts of up to five gigabytes.

Contractors should demonstrate that their products show “significant speed and accuracy improvements in event detection, characterization, and attribution compared to existing baseline systems.”

As skies fill with missiles and drones in conflicts like the ones with Ukraine and Iran, AI is increasingly being seen as an indispensable partner to overworked human operators. In particular, with a perpetual shortage of expensive interceptors , such as the Patriot air-defense system, operators must quickly decide when and where to allocate them.

Defense contractors and AI firms are teaming up to incorporate AI into missile defense.

For example, Northrop Grumman announced in July that it was partnering with AI firm Camgian to incorporate artificial intelligence into integrated air and missile defense systems. BAE and Scale AI have also teamed up for AI-enhanced missile defense.

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

items.title: Saudi crown prince sought US military help with Houthis, sources say
items.author: Samia Nakhoul and Humeyra Pamuk, Reuters
items.summary: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly sought assistance from President Donald Trump on Thursday to help fight Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
items.body:
Pentagon

Saudi crown prince sought US military help with Houthis, sources say

U.S. President Donald Trump meets with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, May 2025. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman sought assistance from U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday to help fight Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter said on Friday, as the Houthis stepped up their threat to the Red Sea.

Trump held at least two phone conversations with the Saudi leader on Thursday, sources said. In the end, Washington told Riyadh that it was not willing to take direct military action for now but would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, the two sources said.

The White House did not address a Reuters question on any phone calls between the two leaders, but a senior administration official speaking on the condition of anonymity said Washington was in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government.

“The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” the official said.

The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the phone calls and conversations between the two leaders.

Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, traveled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for talks, two sources said.

News of the request to Trump was first reported by Axios.

SAUDI APPEAL MARKS CHANGE OF APPROACH

The U.S. war with Iran has entered its seventh month with no immediate end in sight. The war has driven up prices of global oil and U.S. gasoline, sending Trump’s approval ratings to a record low before the November midterm elections.

Houthi control of the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, could give their backer Iran a critical advantage in its war with the U.S., reducing supplies through a second major transit corridor and sending oil prices surging.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea route since the Iran conflict effectively closed Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil used to flow.

The escalation dates back to early July, when the Houthis ⁠said ​their forces confronted Saudi “warplanes” that were attempting ​to prevent an Iranian civilian aircraft from landing at Sanaa International Airport.

But back then, Saudi Arabia told the United States that it could fight the Houthis on its own and emphasized to Washington that the war should not escalate. Saudi officials urged their U.S. counterparts to increase economic pressure on Iran.

The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. ​28, and Iran responded with its own strikes on ​Israel and ⁠Gulf states that host U.S. bases. U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.
