items.title: Air Force BMT Puts Finishing Touches on 1st Airbase Training Range—and Plans for More
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: Under a late summer sun, Air Force basic trainees practice safely rearming a retired F-16 Fighting Falcon at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, with mock AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles. Nearby, a bulldozer levels the ground where the rest of this first new airbase training range will sit. The post Air Force BMT Puts Finishing Touches on 1st Airbase Training Range—and Plans for More appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-LACKLAND, Texas —Under a late summer sun, Air Force basic trainees practice safely rearming a retired F-16 Fighting Falcon here with mock AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles. Nearby, a bulldozer levels the ground where the rest of this first new airbase training range will sit.

If all goes well, two retired C-130 Hercules aircraft that arrived on base in late August will join the F-16 on the mock airbase’s completed tarmac as early as December, Col. Kellie Courtland, commander of the 37th Training Wing that oversees Basic Military Training, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a Sept. 2 interview.

“The goal is to have it ready by December-ish timeframe or early 2027,” Courtland said. “But we’re within months of all of that happening.”

Officials from the 2nd Air Force first revealed plans this past January to inject more realism into Basic Military Training by building mock airbases where future Airmen can get hands-on training with real aircraft. The long-term plan is to have four similar areas each with one F-16 and two C-130s, plus another, more expeditionary training range with dirt airstrips.

The project is part of a sweeping effort in BMT to instill “airmindedness” in new Airmen—making sure they understand the basics of generating airpower, especially if their base falls under attack.

“We want Airmen that are going to rise to the occasion. … What we don’t want is an Airman to say, ‘OK, he’s out of the game, she’s out of the game, and he’s out of the game, therefore the game’s done and we’re not going to do the mission,’” Courtland said. “No, what we want is you to say, ‘She’s out. I may not do her job, but that maintainer that’s over there working, I can hand him the wrenches, or that Airmen that’s got to go out there and fuel that plane now, I can help him pull that hose out and make sure that jet is grounded.’”

Training started on this first F-16 in April. Trainees are tasked with a mission to rearm the fighter, organize into small groups, develop a plan, brief the plan to Military Training Instructors, and complete the mission.

They work out of two containerized training stations on the site that contain training materials: videos and mock AIM-9 missiles and smaller 2.75-inch rockets for the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System.

The mock munitions are much lighter than live ordnance, but MTIs take care to ensure trainees understand it takes three Airmen to carry an AIM-9 and two to carry a 2.75-inch rocket.

“These are training rounds; they’re not weighted … but we highly emphasize the fact that ‘hey, you will do a three-person lift’ just some sense of realism because in reality those missiles weigh about 400 pounds,” said Tech Sgt. Johnny Ngo, an MTI with the 322nd Training Squadron.

Tech. Sgt. Brandon Cruz, an MTI with the 331st Training Squadron, said watching trainees train on a real F-16 brought back the excitement he felt when he went through his technical training to become a loader.

He remembers walking into the hanger, “and there’s these four aircraft out there, and it’s almost a surreal moment; like you feel it in your chest, and I was like, wow, I’m in a Transformers movie or something,” Cruz said. “These trainees are getting that experience in BMT within the first five weeks of actually being here. They’re getting that surreal reality check.”

Tech Sgt. Jeremy Hudson said he remembers how different BMT was when he went through in 2014. “It was the basics—drill, dormitory, and discipline,” the MTI from 322nd said. “It was folding shirts. It was making sure your dormitory and your living area was clean, and then it was drill.”

Trainees coming into BMT now are getting much more realistic training, Hudson said. “Five weeks ago, six weeks ago, they were civilians, and now they get to see an F-16 firsthand,” he said.

Overall, the effort is progressing well, but Courtland, the 37th Training Wing commander, acknowledged there are always logistical hiccups when sorting through multiple changes simultaneously.

“You’re trying to build a new curriculum at the same time, you’re trying to do the construction at the same time, and you’re trying to train the MTIs so that they can train the trainees,” she said. “So, you’re always going to have those little clunky pieces in there, but overall, I think it’s going good, and I think it’s got the support [from the Air Force] it needs to thrust it through.”

When completed, this mock airbase training range will have 16 containerized training stations that trains eight key tasks:

Arming fighter aircraft

Refueling

Casualty transfer and evacuation

Cargo loading

Post-attack and repair

Aircraft marshaling

Aircraft familiarization

Airbase entry control

There is also a much broader plan to grow the airbase into a four-quadrant training range—each with duplicate set-up consisting of two C-130s and an F-16—by 2031, Courtland said.

BMT officials also plan to build a forward airbase training range with a more expeditionary flavor for PACER FORGE , the final field training exercise of BMT that stresses trainees’ agile combat employment skills.

There will be two dirt air strips that intersect and a towable aircraft fuselage, 37th Training Wing Command Chief Master Sgt. Caleb Vaden said, adding that the plan also involves having an F-16 and one C-130. Currently, the simulated airbase at PACER FORGE consists of some hard structures that allow Airmen to practice skills such as perimeter defense.

The forward airbase training range is also scheduled to be completed by 2031, Vaden said.

“It’s going to have a hangar in the middle, so some of those same types of things they’ll be training on here, like well, it’ll split your team up, and hey, some of you are going to be supporting airfield ops. Some of you are going to be supporting a repair team, should there be damage that you have to go out and assess, and those types of things,” Vaden said. “So, it’s just going to be what you have here, forward with reduced resources like we’ve had in real life, and just a lot of chaos going on to really kind of stress them out.”

items.title: Polish prime minister: Poland to develop its own Starlink
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the project will pave the way for the launch of a Starlink-like system for the nation.
items.body:
Europe

Polish prime minister: Poland to develop its own Starlink

Polish soldiers with vehicles are seen during the Defence24 Days exhibition at the National Stadium in Warsaw, Poland, on May 6, 2026. (Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

WARSAW, Poland — Finnish space company ICEYE and Poland’s state-run defense giant PGZ have signed a letter of intent to jointly develop a military satellite communications system.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the project will pave the way for the launch of a Starlink-like system for the nation.

“The culmination of the process that began today can and will be a Polish Starlink,” Tusk said Sept. 9 at the MSPO defense show in Kielce, referring to SpaceX’s satellite network. “Anyone closely following the Russian-Ukrainian war knows how important communications are. It is absolutely critical. Without communications, you have nothing to look for on the modern battlefield.”

In a statement, PGZ said that the program is to be implemented from 2026 to 2030.

ICEYE has an ongoing cooperation with PGZ on an Earth observation system for the Polish Armed Forces. The Finnish company has delivered synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites to the country’s military under its MikroSAR program. The system is designed as the first component of the military space capabilities toolkit Warsaw plans to develop in the coming years. The ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine has fueled Poland’s efforts to ramp up its reconnaissance ability.

“The cooperation is to draw on the experience gained through the MikroSAR program and is to include the development of a space segment based on a distributed architecture, the development of domestic ground infrastructure, and the establishment of industrial capabilities enabling the system to be independently developed and maintained in Poland,” PGZ said.

The Finnish manufacturer said in a statement that its collaboration with the Polish group is to be based on the partners’ complementary roles.

“ICEYE will act as the technology partner, while PGZ will contribute its industrial and organizational capabilities,” the space company said. “ICEYE will be responsible for developing the satellite system architecture, designing and manufacturing the space platforms, and conducting satellite operations. PGZ’s role will be to organize the program’s domestic industrial base by identifying the group’s companies that will contribute their production capabilities, expertise and technical infrastructure.”

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: The Recent Rise of Women Gun Owners
items.summary: In recent years, women made up almost half of all new gun owners, a striking shift from the historical norm, when women accounted for about a quarter of them. And the uptick is widespread across geographic and demographic subgroups.
items.body:
Commentary

Sep 11, 2026

By Rosanna Smart and Andrew R. Morral

This commentary was originally published by Vital City on September 9, 2026.

For generations, gun ownership in America has been a man's world. But that's changing, and fast. Between 2020 and 2022, more than 7.5 million people bought their first gun, and an estimated 60 million new firearms entered the U.S. civilian market. An unprecedented number of these purchasers were women. In recent years, women made up almost half of all new gun owners , a striking shift from the historical norm, when women accounted for about 24% of gun owners. While previous reports on increased gun ownership among women have been overstated , our analysis confirms a notable uptick in female gun ownership that was widespread across geographic and demographic subgroups. What remains unknown are the implications of this trend for public health and safety.

The General Social Survey (GSS) is a large, nationally representative survey of adults in the United States, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago; it has asked about household and personal gun ownership roughly every two years for the past five decades. The GSS also asks about a wide range of social, economic and political measures, supporting descriptions of how ownership trends have varied across subgroups and how the landscape of gun ownership may or may not be changing. (An important note: These are survey data and thus subject to error if people do not know or are unwilling to disclose whether they own guns. But because there are no administrative datasets that capture gun ownership or sales, survey data are the best we have to work with.)

Based on the GSS, women's personal ownership of firearms increased substantially in recent years. After more than a decade of stable gun ownership, women's ownership rose starkly between 2018 and 2021, going from 10% of adult women owning guns in 2018 to 15% in 2021, then up again slightly to 16% by 2024. Other national surveys, such as Pew's American Trends Panel, report similar trends in women's gun ownership over this period (although prevalence estimates differ from GSS, likely due to differences in question wording and sampling). Over the same period, men's gun ownership remained relatively flat; the percentage of men who own guns as of 2024 (36%) is now quite a bit lower than the ownership rate from two decades prior (40%). The result is a continued narrowing of the gender gap in gun ownership, which has fallen from 29 percentage points in 2004 to 19 percentage points in 2024.…

The remainder of this commentary is available at vitalcitynyc.org .

items.title: US refutes claims that Iran captured Saildrone USV
items.author: Claire Barrett
items.summary: A U.S. official denied the video shared by Iran purported to show an American Saildrone USV near the Strait of Hormuz in flames.
items.body:
MilTech

US refutes claims that Iran captured Saildrone USV

Since 2023, Saildrone’s USVs have worked in coordination with the U.S. Navy. (Saildrone)

A video shared by Iran Wednesday purported to show an American Saildrone unmanned surface vessel near the Strait of Hormuz in flames after being attacked by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has been making the rounds on social media.

U.S. officials disputed that claim.

“All of our Saildrones are accounted for and fully operational,” an official told Military Times.

The video comes on the heels of another incident in which an Anduril Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle — designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions — was captured on Sept. 8.

U.S. Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins of U.S. Central Command told Reuters that the “defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment.”

“Of course Iran will take every opportunity as a propaganda win,” Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told the outlet. “It can help the (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) make better versions of their own designs.”

The Navy recently awarded Saildrone Voyager a $16.3 million task order to extend operations of the Voyager fleet in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, according to an August release .

Since 2023, Saildrone’s USVs have worked in coordination with the U.S. Navy, supporting the Joint Interagency Task Force South, or JIATF-S, and U.S. Naval Forces Southern Command/U.S. Navy Fourth Fleet, per the release.

The 33-foot-long Voyager is designed for persistent surface and subsurface surveillance and can also conduct nearshore mapping missions and seafloor characterization.

Able to remain “on mission and on station” for months at a time, the USVs are “both a deterrent and an alarm” along the U.S.’s expansive southern maritime border, according to the company.

Claire Barrett is an editor and military history correspondent for Military Times. She is also a World War II researcher with an unparalleled affinity for Sir Winston Churchill and Michigan football.

items.title: German military eyes cruise missiles from Covenant, a surprise vendor setting up shop
items.author: Linus Höller
items.summary: The German military is in talks with Covenant over the company's Anthem cruise missile, the country’s defense ministry said on Friday.
items.body:
Europe

German military eyes cruise missiles from Covenant, a surprise vendor setting up shop

Anthem, a long-range cruise missile carrying a heavy payload, makes a test flight at a range of defense startup Covenant at an undisclosed location June 30, 2026. (Covenant/Handout via Reuters)

VIENNA — The German military is in talks with Covenant, a U.S.-Israeli, venture capital-backed startup, over its Anthem cruise missile, the country’s defense ministry said on Friday.

The weapon could presumably help close a gap quickly in Berlin’s long-range strike arsenal, meant to deter Russian aggression. That weapons portfolio is considered shaky, as a new version of the go-to air-launched Taurus cruise missile is years away from fielding, envisioned U.S. deliveries of Tomahawk cruise missiles are iffy after heavy use in the American-Israeli war against Iran, and a pan-European development effort, dubbed ELSA, is just getting off the ground.

A German Defense Ministry spokesperson declined to provide additional information about the state of negotiations with Covenant beyond saying they were ongoing, or about how the Anthem would fit into Bundeswehr planning. So far, Germany has put Lockheed Martin-made Typhon launchers front and center in the military’s envisioned ground-based strike ecosystem. The launchers can fire a variety of munitions of varying ranges, including Tomahawks, which can fly more than 1,500 kilometers.

Anthem, too, is reportedly ground launched, though the company did not respond in time for publication on the details of its launch system.

Covenant claims the Anthem weapon is production-ready, and flight tests are taking place weekly. The company’s pitch is that it can produce missiles more cheaply than current standard systems. Reuters has previously reported a mid-six-figure target price per unit set by company executives during serial production. A current-generation Taurus missile costs $1 million or more.

The company was founded in 2024 and chose to operate in “stealth mode” for two years until the announcement this week. It employs 200 people, according to reporting by Reuters, and was recruiting for 29 positions, seven of them in Germany, at the time of writing.

According to the company’s website, “Anthem is built on local production lines so allied governments buy directly from an industrial base they can rely on.”

In local media, the facility in Germany has been identified as sitting in an industrial neighborhood on the north side of the Saxon city of Leipzig, near the major Leipzig-Halle Airport. Asked for specifics, the company declined to provide further information, saying only said it was leasing an existing building.

Serial production is set to begin in Germany at the beginning of 2027, according to a Berlin lobbying firm handling local media inquiries on behalf of Covenant. A spokesman there told Defense News in an email that “global customers” would receive Anthems “as early as 2026, but German-built Anthems will begin in Q1 2027,” short-hand for the first quarter of next year.

The company’s main facility is located in Grand Prairie, Texas. A third plant is in Israel.

Reuters had previously reported German production for an unnamed non-American recipient starting by the end of the year, citing company executives.

German online publication Tag24 has reported that the facility in Leipzig will not handle explosives, allowing it to operate under regulations as a metalworking plant rather than a munitions factory. Asked by Defense News, the company declined to provide further details about where propellant and warhead integration would take place for European-produced units, and whether this would be done within Germany or elsewhere.

Similarly, Covenant declined to provide any indication of who potential European buyers might be.

The announcement of the Leipzig-area facility comes at a politically sensitive time in east Germany, with the far-right alternative for Germany party winning majorities in local elections, most recently in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt last weekend. The party, which is close with Russia and opposes support for Ukraine, is also the strongest political force in Saxony itself, where the Covenant facility is to be located.

In its public messaging, AfD has often billed itself as a party of peace. At the same time, the party advocates for a strong military and defense industry – as long as Russian interests are untouched.

Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Ulrich Siegmund, who led the AfD to victory in Saxony-Anhalt, said his party was not fundamentally opposed to arms makers.

“We do not demonize the production of military equipment across the board, because we will, of course, need the necessary auxiliary means for later remigration and deportation campaigns,” he said, using a political catchphrase favored by right-wing parties across Europe.

In Saxony-Anhalt, where Siegmund hopes to become governor following his election victory, a new facility by the Israeli company Elbit Systems has caused controversy and was the impetus for his remarks.

Local and regional AfD branches in Leipzig and Saxony have criticized the plans for the opening of the Covenant facility in their jurisdiction.

Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

items.title: Who Benefits from Education Savings Accounts? Q&A with Susha Roy
items.summary: Tens of thousands of American families use state-funded education savings accounts for their children's education. How exactly do these accounts work? Who benefits from them? And how do they affect education funding more broadly?
items.body:
Who Benefits from Education Savings Accounts? Q&A with Susha Roy

Commentary

Sep 11, 2026

Tens of thousands of American families have some decisions to make as a new school year begins. They hold state-funded education savings accounts, which give them wide latitude to choose how to educate their children.

Such accounts have been around for years, mostly as a way to help students with disabilities get the specialized services they need. But a growing number of states have made them available to all families. Federal tax credits kicking in this year will also allow families to write off up to $1,700 to scholarship-granting organizations for similar education services and expenses.

What all this will mean for students, their academic achievement, and the future of public schools is still far from clear.

Susha Roy has been looking for answers in one of the states that pioneered education savings accounts, Arizona. She’s a policy researcher at RAND and a specialist in school choice policies. Her findings could help other states ensure their programs are helping the students they want to help, without leaving some behind.

Let’s start with the basics. What are education savings accounts, and how do they work?

They essentially take the money that would have been allocated for a student in public school and make it available directly to the family. The family can then use it on any sort of educational expense. That could be private school tuition, tutoring services, homeschooling expenses, textbooks—you name it.

Your research has shown that these accounts can be game changers for some students. Who benefits from them?

There are two main categories of students who have typically benefited from these. The first is students in underperforming neighborhood schools. These accounts give them the flexibility to pursue something outside of their local public school, and that can be really important for them.

The other category is students with disabilities. There are all kinds of special needs that public schools are very well equipped to support. But there are also disabilities that require very individualized and specialized support. Our research in Arizona found that a large number of students with autism use these accounts, for example. The support they need can be so varied that public schools might not be able to meet their needs. These accounts may be really helpful for them.

There have also been concerns about “cream skimming” as states make these accounts available to everyone. What is that, and how might these accounts encourage it?

Cream skimming is when private schools and other schools of choice enroll students who are higher achieving or more affluent or just easier to educate than the general student population. We found a pretty clear pattern of this in Arizona: Students using these accounts tended to live in wealthier neighborhoods and came from higher-achieving public school districts. They weren’t necessarily reflective of the population of students who you might think could benefit the most from these education savings accounts.

Now, early adopters of any education program are often different from the general population. But what this does suggest to me is that policy design is really important here. We shouldn’t expect that all kids and families will know how to take advantage of these new accounts. If states want to expand access to educational opportunities for all students, they could consider prioritizing outreach to families who could benefit the most.

If states want to expand access to educational opportunities for all students, they could consider prioritizing outreach to families who could benefit the most.

How do these accounts affect funding for public schools and the broader education system?

Most states tie state funding for public schools to student enrollment. So if students opt out of going to their public school, that is going to decrease the state funds the school will receive. Maybe the school can save money by not hiring as many teachers, since it won’t have as many students. But it still has fixed costs, like building maintenance, and that can become a real challenge.

What we saw in Arizona, though, was that a lot of the students who received these accounts were already in private school. And we found evidence that private school tuition went up when these accounts became available. We need more research here, but it could be that schools raised their tuition to try to capture the additional state funding that families had coming in.

It goes back to how you design these programs. If there are no accountability mechanisms, you might just inflate the cost of private school and subsidize families whose kids were already going to private school anyway without making sure the quality of those schools also improves.

If you were advising state leaders who were considering accounts like these, what would you tell them?

Collect data on how students with these accounts perform in their receiving schools. Without that, we just won’t know for sure whether the money states spend on education savings accounts benefits children.

I’ve had some encouraging conversations with some states that are trying to be really thoughtful about this. A few have talked about having a student ID that stays with students as they move between sectors. That would allow you to track student outcomes in a way that we really can’t right now.

It’s critically important that states’ highly consequential policy decisions are informed by good evidence. That’s why we do this work at RAND. There’s such a huge opportunity to help states shape these important policy decisions so they benefit their constituents.

items.title: The Military Court Service
items.summary: The Military Court Service provides a criminal court for the Royal Navy, Army and Royal Air Force in the Court Martial, Summary Appeal and Service Civilian Court.
items.body:
Introduction

The Military Court Service ( MCS ) works closely with, but is independent of: the Office of the Judge Advocate General ; the Service Prosecuting Authority , which is equivalent to the Crown Prosecution Service; the Service chains of command, Service and MOD personnel branches; the National Probation Service ; and the victim and witness services and military court advocates.

Service Court proceedings are publicised over a two-week assize period. Military court listings. All hearings are open to the public in exactly the same way as civilian courts, unless otherwise directed by the presiding judge.

Service Court results are now published on a monthly basis.

Further information on the Court Martial, Summary Appeal Court and the Service Civilian Court can be found in the Manual of Service Law JSP 830.

HM Crown Prosecution Service Inspectorate - Military Court Service Report - August 2026

This inspection was undertaken at the invitation of the Director of the Military Court Service. Such invitations reflect a commitment to transparency, continuous improvement and independent scrutiny. I welcome the willingness of the MCS to subject itself to external inspection and to seek assurance about the effectiveness and efficiency of the service it provides. This is reflective of a positive approach and demonstrates a mature organisation with a culture that is open to challenge and improvement.

Anthony Rogers HM Chief Inspector of the Crown Prosecution Service

HMCPSI - The Military Court Service, August 2026

Organisation

The MCS is independent of the Service chains of command and is staffed by civil servants employed by the Ministry of Defence ( MOD ) working from both court centres.

To ensure independence, the Director MCS is appointed by the Defence Council as the Court Administration Officer ( CAO ). The CAO has a legislated function to give notice of court proceedings and to specify lay members of the court (equivalent to jury selection).

The Court Martial Appeal Court recently clarified the respective roles of the Judge Advocate and the CAO in relation to the constitution of the Court Martial, concluding that the Judge Advocate’s role is to give direction on the composition category, while the CAO is responsible for specifying individual members. These duties are conducted in accordance with the Armed Forces Act 2006 and related Statutory Instruments.

Court of Appeal Judgment - Rex v B ( PDF , 116 KB , 15 pages )

Court of Appeal Judgment - Rex v B - Odt ( ODT , 38.4 KB )

The CAO is a permanent member of both the Service Justice Board (SJB) and the Service Justice Executive Group (SJEG).

The Director MCS operates from the Bulford Court Centre supported by a Senior Management Team and a Court Administration Unit. Each Court Centre has a dedicated Court Officer who is directly responsible for the management of court proceedings, liaison with the Judiciary and court listings.

The current Director of the Military Court Service is Mr Cleaven Faulkner JP:

Cleaven Faulkner JP - Biography ( PDF , 150 KB , 1 page )

Military Court Service Strategic Plan 2026-2030

The Strategic Plan, owned by the Director of the Military Court Service ( MCS ), sets the direction for MCS personnel and partners in delivering Military Court business.

The Service Justice System is a vital public service relied upon by hundreds of victims, witnesses, families, and defendants across the UK and overseas to deliver justice outcomes that matter.

Building on the achievements of the past four years, this plan provides a clear roadmap for delivering an operating model centred on timely, impartial, and efficient administration of Service court proceedings. It aims to strengthen confidence in a justice system that is fair, effective, and accessible to all who depend upon it.

The strategy drives a culture of continuous improvement and ongoing modernisation of our court processes. It recognises the value of embracing technology‑based systems that enhance efficiency, reduce duplication and bureaucracy, and improve integration with our partners and stakeholders. These reforms lay the groundwork for MCS to deliver a new fully integrated Military Court Listing System (MCLS), with its incumbent in‑court digital case management system, Case Center.

Following significant investment in recent years, the MCS is now well placed to consolidate progress, continue to adopt innovative technologies and ensure that the Services have a modern, effective court system that works in the interests of all Service personnel and their families. Looking ahead to 2030, the strategy identifies the areas in which the MCS will continue to modernise and transform, ensuring best value for money and delivering an increasingly efficient and effective criminal court service for the Royal Navy, the Army, and the Royal Air Force.

Through this modernisation, we aim to build greater confidence in and respect for the Service Justice System. We are committed to continue our work in building a leading‑edge service that is open, inclusive, and innovative. Success will be delivered through the professionalism, dedication, and integrity of our people, who work every day to uphold the principles of justice.

MCS Strategic Plan 2026-2030 ( PDF , 249 KB , 7 pages )

Military Court Centres

There are two permanent court centres in the UK. Bulford, Wiltshire and Catterick, North Yorkshire.

A view of the Bulford Military Court Centre

A view of the Catterick Court (BSL Version)

Military Court Centre information and images of our court rooms.

Due to the draw down of British Forces Germany, the permanent court centre at Sennelager has been converted for other use but has been retained as a Court Martial location should one be required. MCS have a permanent Court Martial capability at Episkopi, Cyprus.

The court system is entirely portable, with the ability for MCS to convene trials outside of the MCCs anywhere in the UK or elsewhere. The most recent examples have included Nightingale Courts at Tidworth and Catterick and overseas in Cyprus, Germany and Gibraltar.

MCS have invested in the latest Digital Audio Recording (DAR) technology to meet legal compliance for the recording of proceedings. The capability covers both the four fixed courts and two portable recording equipment sets. The Service Courts have the latest Digital Evidential Presentation System and now have the capability to support the pre-recording of evidence from victims of serious sexual assault (Section 28).

The Service Courts have a state-of-the-art case management system called Case Center. This product is the latest version of the Crown Court system, Caselines and has been operational since September 2023. MCS are moving towards completing the last element of its digital transformation program with Board members using laptops to view evidence, via the Case Center Jury Portal, during proceedings.

Procedure

The Deputy Director MCS oversees the delivery of the MCS assize programme. Cases are listed within ‘assize sessions’, held at the Military Court Centres run by MCS staff. However, a particularly lengthy or complex Court Martial or Service Civilian Court case may be listed as a ‘stand-alone’ outside the assize sessions. Where possible the volume of cases is equally split between both Court Centres.

At the listing phase of case management, the Court officer will work with the resident Judge Advocate to appoint a Judge Advocate to each case.

The MCS policy is to list a case for an initial hearing within 42 days after receipt of directional papers from the Service Prosecuting Authority.

How we select a Court Martial Board

Our Operating procedure for selecting Court Martial Boards

Court Martial Board Standard Operating Procedure ( PDF , 304 KB , 21 pages ) .

On 1 January 2023 legislation delivered changes to the constitution of a Court Martial board. The changes required the CAO to specify Court Martial boards with at least one man and one woman (so far as is reasonably practicable) and to specify an increase from five lay members to six, for proceedings of a prescribed description. Specification of the OR7 rank from the nominated pool of lay members may now also be permitted under the act.

‘OR7 rank’ means any of the following— chief petty officer, staff corporal, staff sergeant, colour sergeant, Royal Marines, flight sergeant, chief technician.

The Armed Forces (Service Court Rules) (Amendment) (No. 2) Rules 2022

Section 155, Armed Forces Act 2006

The Military Court Service case management system, Case Center (formerly Caselines)

The Military Court Service partners with Thomson Reuters using Case Center. The application streamlines the way the courts prepare, manage, and present digital cases within a centralised cloud-based solution.

The court will manage proceedings by sending and sharing case materials from any device, keeping all parties in sync as they prepare for a hearing. In a hearing, purpose-built presentation tools streamlines proceedings so parties can direct others to the right document in a timely manner.

Appearing as a legal representative in a Military Court

If you are appearing as a legal representative in a Military Court you will need to create a Case Center account using the link below. Please read and understand the application terms and conditions for use and the acceptable use policy before registering.

Case Center - terms and conditions for use and acceptable use policy ( PDF , 105 KB , 2 pages )

After you enter your details and the role you will be performing within the Service Justice System you will be registered and ready to be invited to your allocated cases.

Register - Thomson Reuters Case Center

Once you have been verified by the Military Court Service either directly with the court, or with the Armed Forces Criminal legal Aid Authority, you will be invited to the case. This process mirrors that applied by the Ministry of Justice in the use for the Digital Case System (DCS).

MCS Case Center User Guide ( PDF , 2.16 MB , 13 pages )

Where to assign documents on Case Center ( PDF , 181 KB , 2 pages ) .

Where to assign documents on Case Center ( ODT , 9.56 KB ) .

Court Martial and Summary Appeal Court Guidance

Guides are issued under the authority of the Judge Advocate General and the Director of the Military Court Service jointly as an aid to those who practise in the Service Justice System, and it is to be used in all hearings. Volume 1 provides information about procedure generally and it deals with all types of proceedings in the Court Martial as well as in the Summary Appeal Court. Volume 2 provides information specifically for members of boards.

Court Martial and Summary Appeal Court Guide Vol 1 - January 2026 ( PDF , 354 KB , 16 pages )

Court Martial and Summary Appeal Court Guide Vol 2 - January 2026 ( PDF , 280 KB , 15 pages )

Guidance on practice, procedure and sentencing is issued by the Judge Advocate General .

Court Martial Appeal Court

The Court Martial Appeal Court, convened for the very first time at the Catterick Military Court Centre on 9 June 2026.

The proceedings involved four cases presided over by the Rt Hon Lord Justice Edis, Mr Justice Griffiths and Mrs Justice Norton.

The Court Martial Appeal Court, sat at the Bulford Military Court Centre for the first time on 4 December 2024.

The day’s proceedings involved three cases presided over by the Rt Hon Lord Justice Holroyde, Mr Justice Morris and Mrs Justice Foster.

Apply for a transcript of a Service Court hearing

Service Court hearings are always recorded. You can apply for a transcript of a Service Court hearing. The court can refuse to provide part or all of a transcript (for example, if details of the hearing are confidential).

If you wish to apply for a transcript you may download and fill in a Transcript request form ( MS Word Document , 50.5 KB ) .

Once completed, email your application to mcs-group@mod.gov.uk .

Transcripts may attract a financial cost unless you are a party to proceedings.

Sentencing remarks in the Court Martial

Transcripts of the judge advocate’s sentencing remarks in cases heard after 1 January 2025 in which the sentence includes dismissal from His Majesty’s Service will be considered for publication by the Judge Advocate General. If published, transcripts will remain on the page for up to 12 months from the date of conviction.

Court Martial sentencing remarks 2025

Court Martial sentencing remarks 2026

Section 28 Edits Form ( MS Word Document , 40.1 KB ) .

Section 28 Edits Form - ODT ( ODT , 23.1 KB ) .

Remote observation of Service Court proceedings

Open justice has been a fundamental principle for centuries. The principle is a broad one, but at its core has always been a right of access to a public hearing. Historically, this has meant access for reporters and other members of the public to the court or other room in which the hearing takes place.

The primary legislation is contained in section 85A of the Courts Act 2003 as inserted by section 198 of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022. The regime is implemented by the Remote Observation and Recording (Courts and Tribunals) Regulations 2022. The power is to “direct that images or sounds of the proceedings be transmitted electronically”. It is to be exercised “for the purpose of enabling persons not taking part in the proceedings to watch or listen to” them. It is not designed for those taking part in the proceedings.

Any person wishing to make an application to the Military Court Service to request permission for the remote observation of a hearing can do so:

Applicants must ensure the court are given at least 3 clear working days to process applications.

items.title: Military Court Centres
items.summary: The Service Justice System is supported in the UK by two designated Military Court Centres at Bulford (Wiltshire) and Catterick (North Yorkshire).
items.body:
Hearings at both court centres are open to the public unless directed otherwise by a Judge Advocate.

The courts are located on the perimeter of a military establishment. This design provides public access to the Service Courts. The public entrance is staffed by the personnel from Military Provost Guard Service who employ security screening checks as a condition of entry.

Each court centre has two court rooms with all courts holding the capability to manage any type of case within the Service Justice System. Case are listed between the hours of 9.30am to 4.30pm, Monday to Friday. The courts do not sit on Saturdays, Sundays and on public holidays.

Each court is fitted with the latest Digital Audio Recording technology, Assistive Listening devices, Digital AV/IP Evidential Presentation Systems and the latest Section 28 recording capability. We are leading the use of in-court technology for the Board members and defendants and are developing our use of AI court transcription technology throughout 2025.

items.title: India puts domestic industry at heart of new military equipment orders
items.author: Anjana Pasricha
items.summary: India will source nearly all of $11.6 billion worth of recently approved military hardware from domestic manufacturers, the government said.
items.body:
Asia Pacific

India puts domestic industry at heart of new military equipment orders

Army personnel display military equipment to students during a defense exhibition in Amritsar, India, on Aug. 31, 2026. (Narinder Nanu / AFP via Getty Images)

NEW DELHI — India will source nearly all of $11.6 billion worth of recently approved military hardware from domestic manufacturers, underscoring New Delhi’s push to reduce dependence on foreign arms suppliers as it modernizes its armed forces.

The Defense Acquisition Council headed by Defense Minister Rajnath Singh granted “in principle” approval, which is essentially a green light to begin the procurement process.

“Approximately 98% of procurements will be made from the Indian Industry,” a Defense Ministry statement said on Monday.

The ambitious goal to source nearly all of the latest round of military acquisitions domestically comes amid a significant shift in government policy. After years of relying heavily on state-owned firms for defense production, India, the world’s fifth largest military spender, has encouraged a larger role for the private sector as part of efforts to build a more dynamic military industrial base.

The latest military equipment approvals span all three services and cover a broad range of equipment. For the Army, they include advanced light helicopters, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear reconnaissance vehicles, mine-laying vehicles, high mobility vehicles and portable bridges to cross rivers and difficult terrain.

The Navy will get new surveillance radars to replace aging systems at naval air stations. The approvals also include funding to design and develop marine gas turbines domestically. India builds its own warships but still imports propulsion systems from overseas suppliers – a gap seen as a major strategic vulnerability.

The Air Force acquisitions include a ground-based multi-purpose jammer for electronic warfare and unspecified equipment to enhance the war-fighting capability of fighter jets, transport aircraft and helicopters.

The funds will be allocated from the $86 billion annual defense budget approved earlier this year.

The involvement of private industry in defense manufacturing has helped India increase the share of equipment produced domestically and reduce reliance on imports. The government says roughly 65% of India’s military hardware is now produced domestically, marking a major reversal from a decade ago when that same share -- about two-thirds of its military hardware—was imported.

Nearly a quarter of the approximately $20 billion worth of defense equipment produced in the last fiscal year, 2025–26, came from private companies.

Pointing out that private industry brings efficiency, research capabilities and a greater willingness to take risks, Defense Minister Singh said earlier this year that the country aims to increase its share in defense production to 50%.

Private defense companies now manufacture everything from radars, artillery guns, armored vehicles, missiles and ammunition to drones, small arms, aerostructures and naval systems, expanding into areas once dominated by state-owned manufacturers.

The emphasis on domestic manufacturing aims to reduce the country’s strategic vulnerability to foreign suppliers and ensure that the military can replenish equipment and weapons faster during hostilities. Observers, however, point out that some of this equipment such as drones, uses several imported components like sensors and avionics, making the country still dependent on foreign technology and supply chains.

India also continues to rely heavily on foreign suppliers for several key military platforms such as fighter jets.

PDF , 97.8 KB , 4 pages

Details

In line with the government’s transparency and open data initiative, the Military Court Service is to publish the court listings for the military court centres.

Each court listing covers the next one or two week assize period. This will be published on the internet by the last working day in advance of the assize period.

In addition to this, the court listings are published using digital signage technology within the reception areas of both military court centres.

Please be aware that the court listings are subject to change after publication, if you wish to find out more please contact the relevant military court centre. Details can be found at the bottom of each court listing.

items.title: GA-ASI’s Uncrewed Combat Aviation Portfolio Answers Call for High-End Warfare Capability
items.author: admin
items.summary: General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI), the company that introduced the world to unmanned warfare, has systematically transformed its aircraft lineup to address the defining requirements of modern high-technology warfare: range, persistence, payload, survivability, and scale against advanced adversaries. The... The post GA-ASI’s Uncrewed Combat Aviation Portfolio Answers Call for High-End Warfare Capability appeared first on <a href="ht
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI) , the company that introduced the world to unmanned warfare, has systematically transformed its aircraft lineup to address the defining requirements of modern high-technology warfare: range, persistence, payload, survivability, and scale against advanced adversaries.

The portfolio now spans from the company’s enhanced MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian platforms capable of long-range maritime strike, to the expeditionary Mojave STOL , to the Air Force’s newly selected FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) — its first uncrewed fighter — and, most recently, to the Wildfire Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA) , a theater-range platform engineered for affordable, attrition-tolerant combat mass.

According to GA-ASI President David Alexander, the United States has entered an era where winning demands large, capable Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) that can operate from friendly airspace into contested environments affordably, without risking aircrews.

“We’ve never been a company that rested on its laurels,” said Alexander. “The conversation around uncrewed systems has changed, and frankly, it should. The battlefield has evolved, threats have evolved, and so have we.

“We’re keeping ahead of the game, and, in the case of our FQ-42A and Wildfire aircraft, we’ve designed them from the start to overmatch threats today and into the future.”

Physics Demands Large Airframes

Losses in contested environments have prompted some observers to suggest moving away from large UAS platforms. Alexander sees those same operations as validation for continued investment in evolved large UAS.

“Yes, we’ve seen combat losses,” he said. “We’ve also heard Pentagon leaders call our Reaper the ‘MVP’ of the campaign. That tells you something important. When a system consistently delivers decisive effects, you modernize it and build on it. And I believe that’s where the Department of War is headed.”

Alexander emphasized that Reaper was purpose-built to provide persistent surveillance, long endurance, and precision strike. MQ-9A delivers these capabilities at scale and at a fraction of the cost of manned platforms that put pilots’ lives at risk, he added.

The proliferation of small drones — quadcopters, gliders, and short-range rockets — doesn’t change fundamental operational requirements, he said.

Despite the hype, smaller platforms “can’t change physics,” Alexander noted.

“Long-range, high-payload, high-endurance missions require large, hefty airframes with significant wingspan, fuel capacity, and payload volume,” he continued. “If we are serious about surveilling and targeting across wide ocean areas, tracking mobile missile units, and holding adversary assets at risk from standoff distances, large UAS modernized for contested environments are the decisive advantage.”

Wildfire: Delivering Attritable Mass at Theater Range

Wildfire represents GA-ASI’s answer to a critical requirement: affordable combat mass that can sustain losses while maintaining operational pressure across contested theaters.

This theater-range, high-production UAS is designed specifically for high-threat environments:

Combat payload and range: Wildfire can carry two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles (LRASM) or four Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) for meaningful combat distances and has a ferry range that exceeds 8,000 nautical miles. This enables delivery of weapons, sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, or communications relay deep into contested battlespace.

Modular architecture: Open interfaces and modular payload hard points enable modularity to support rapid mission reconfiguration, allowing commanders to adapt as threats and priorities shift during operations.

Volume production: Leveraging more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing capacity and advanced production processes, Wildfire is engineered to be built and fielded in numbers sufficient to absorb attrition while maintaining persistent theater-wide pressure.

Combined with Gambit Series capabilities, Wildfire delivers what defense leaders call “attritable mass”— large numbers of capable systems whose loss does not constitute strategic setback because they are affordable, uncrewed, and replaceable.

Gambit Series: Autonomous Combat Jets for Peer Threats

The Gambit Series represents GA-ASI’s family of autonomous jets for high-end contested operations. Built around a common core comprising roughly 70 percent of key components, the platform’s modular architecture drives down costs while simplifying production, logistics, and sustainment.

Recently selected by the U.S. Air Force for its CCA program, the FQ-42A — designed to fly alongside fighters like the F-22 — is a variant of GA-ASI’s Gambit 2.

Across six missionized Gambit variants, the architecture supports:

Long-endurance ISR in contested airspace

Air-to-air combat

Adversary training for advanced threat replication

Stealth reconnaissance in denied areas

Carrier-based naval operations

Penetrating air-to-ground strike and suppression of enemy air defenses

All Gambit aircraft are designed for human-machine teaming with advanced fighters and other UAS, extending sensors, adding weapons capacity, and imposing complex targeting dilemmas on adversary defenses — precisely the type of effects envisioned in modern Air Force operational concepts.

Mojave STOL: Airpower, Hold the Tarmac

Built on GA-ASI’s other pioneering aircraft, Mojave STOL addresses a critical vulnerability in modern combat: dependence on large runways.

Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) capability: Mojave STOL operates from austere, unprepared locations — open fields, dry riverbeds, even amphibious assault ship decks — generating uncrewed combat airpower from sites adversaries cannot easily target or predict.

Advanced sensor integration: Controllable via human-portable, laptop-based ground control systems, Mojave STOL carries cutting-edge radar, electro-optical/infrared, and signals intelligence payloads, providing a comprehensive operational picture for precise targeting and situational awareness to support dispersed forces.

In a combat environment where large runways are vulnerable to adversary strikes, Mojave STOL establishes airfields without airports. Its rugged construction enables persistent ISR and strike capability sourced from improvised mobile launch and recovery sites.

MQ-9B: Evolved Flagship Platform for Standoff Operations

MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian remain GA-ASI’s flagship multi-mission ISR platforms, now upgraded for long-range contested operations and integration into distributed kill chains.

Long-range weapons integration: New pylons with 30-inch lug spacing accommodate larger standoff munitions, including LRASM and JSM. Combined with MQ-9B’s advanced ISR suite, this transforms the aircraft into a long-range strike and maritime interdiction platform capable of engaging far outside adversary standoff ranges.

Resilient communications: Integration with proliferated Low Earth Orbit (pLEO) satellite constellations provides low-latency, high-bandwidth, jam-resistant connectivity. In combination with DoD-standard cybersecurity, MQ-9B maintains secure command-and-control and sensor links globally, even under electronic attack.

For Air Force and joint planners, MQ-9B has evolved beyond counterinsurgency roots into a standoff sensor-shooter that functions as a resilient node in distributed operations.

Urgency Driven by Evolving Threats

Alexander noted that changing battlefield conditions have continually driven the company to advance its technology and operational concepts.

“When you look at the threats we’re seeing in Ukraine and Iran, we already knew our aircraft would need to evolve, and we’ve been pushing ahead there for years now,” he said. “But it seems like every morning the news puts fresh urgency behind delivering that vital combat capability while finding ways to strip out some of what drives up costs.”

That urgency is backed by unmatched operational experience. To date, GA-ASI has accumulated nearly 10 million flight hours, the vast majority in combat operations.

Taken as a whole, Alexander said, the aircraft portfolio shows that GA-ASI is serious about retaining its position as the leading provider of UAS to the United States and its allies.

“We know, to our core, what it takes to deliver relevant systems,” he said. “We have the people, infrastructure, and capacity in place, today, to do it at scale.

“GA-ASI is ready to answer the call.”

items.title: Public procurement and AI governance
items.author: Afek Shamir
items.summary: This report examines how AI middle powers can use public procurement to govern frontier AI. It develops a set of procurement guarantees, and assesses whether coordinated purchasing standards could strengthen state bargaining power.
items.body:
This report assesses public procurement as an AI governance tool, develops contractual guarantees for state buyers, and examines whether coordination among AI middle powers could strengthen bargaining leverage, evaluation capacity and resilience to AI crises.

Public procurement and AI governance

Developing a strategic framework for middle powers

Afek Shamir

Research Published Sep 11, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Frontier AI capabilities are concentrated among a small number of private firms headquartered in the United States and China. For states which neither develop nor host leading models, this concentration creates a dependence on foreign AI providers whose capabilities they often cannot independently evaluate and whose technology may be constrained by the laws of the provider’s home jurisdiction.

Public procurement offers ‘AI middle powers’ one mechanism for governing these dependencies. These are states with significant economic, diplomatic, security or regulatory capabilities that nevertheless depend technologically on foreign frontier AI firms. The report finds that three categories of risk fall disproportionately on state buyers in AI middle powers : vendor lock-in and the threat of service withdrawal, limited visibility into frontier AI development, and data sovereignty and information-security risks.

To mitigate these risks, the report develops a framework of procurement obligations that governments could seek to negotiate with AI providers. These include model access for evaluation, information sharing, funding for reliability research, state-of-the-art risk management requirements, termination and exit provisions, and measures to support domestic and allied capability.

The analysis finds that public procurement is a useful but bounded mechanism for governing frontier AI. Governments are not yet major customers of frontier AI firms, and leading developers may be able to forego government contracts rather than accept costly requirements. Procurement contracts with foreign providers may also remain subordinate to the national-security laws of a vendor’s home state, and state buyers can face persistent information asymmetries when negotiating with leading technology companies. At the same time, government demand for frontier AI is growing, and public-sector contracts offer firms more than revenue alone. They provide financial predictability and a degree of prestige and regulatory validation, making governments strategically important customers even if they are not yet indispensable to firms’ business models.

The central recommendation is that AI middle powers should assess whether collective coordination on procurement requirements can strengthen their bargaining position and state capacity.

Key Takeaways

Short-term actions (actions that could be initiated within 12 months):

Firstly, governments should begin with a shared assessment of the risks that procurement requirements are intended to address. Participating states should compare the risks they associate with different government uses of frontier AI, including but not limited to dependence on individual foreign providers, loss of access, insufficient visibility into model behaviour, and requirements for data control. Common procurement provisions should follow predominantly where separate governments assess risks similarly.

Secondly, governments should assess the most suitable institutional arrangement for procurement coordination. The G7, the EU, NATO, and International Network of AI Safety Institutes already provide mechanisms for cooperation on AI policy, standards and technical evaluation. A dedicated arrangement may be justified where no current institution combines sufficient purchasing relevance and technical capacity.

Thirdly, smaller middle powers which lack state access to frontier AI should explore opportunities to pool demand with partners and strengthen their negotiating position. Where an individual government is unlikely to represent sufficient demand to influence a frontier AI provider, cooperation with other buyers could increase the commercial significance of their purchasing preferences and requirements.

Medium- to long-term actions (actions likely to require approximately 1–5 years or longer):

Firstly, governments should identify which AI capabilities need to remain available independently of any single foreign provider and invest selectively in the infrastructure required to preserve them. For most middle powers, this is unlikely to mean reproducing the full frontier AI stack nationally. A more realistic strategy could include building a meaningful share of domestic or allied compute, creating secure hosting facilities, securing access to multiple model families for optionality reasons, and bringing in technical talent to government with expertise in fine-tuning and the know-how to migrate critical workloads. These assets would also strengthen bargaining power by making the future option of switching providers more credible.

Secondly, governments should strengthen their capacity to evaluate and assure frontier AI systems. This includes developing assurance and technical AI expertise within defence agencies and supporting the creation of a mature third-party evaluation and assurance sector. These capabilities are necessary to make procurement guarantees practically enforceable.

Thirdly, procurement coordination could provide a basis for wider cooperation on AI incidents and resilience to AI-related failures. Governments that establish common procurement requirements would have an existing mechanism for sharing information with one another and with providers. Over time, this could support common approaches to incident reporting and exercises for responding to significant AI-related incidents.

Strategic guidance from the command in charge of Air Force training lays out a plan to train all Airmen in artificial intelligence and build “Digital Airmen” across the force’s training and education enterprise.

Lt. Gen. Clack J. Quinn, the head of Air Education and Training Command, signed the directive Aug. 17, according to a release from AETC this week. It’s meant to serve as a blueprint for how AETC will integrate AI into all of its training, from pilot education to technical training.

The goal is to reduce average time-to-train by up to 20 percent in targeted technical specialties using competency-based, adaptive learning and lowering standards, AETC spokesman Daniel Hawkins told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email response.

“Traditional training often adheres to fixed time schedules regardless of individual learner grasp,” Hawkins wrote. “AI-augmented courseware adapts to the student’s pace in real time, providing immediate personalized instruction, targeted remediation, and immersive repetition where needed. Airmen must still demonstrate 100% mastery of established foundational and specialty standards before graduating.”

During the implementation phase, the command will evaluate specific initial career fields and demonstration detachments to use the new AI-enabled learning tools and approaches, he said.

“Initial prototype candidates for AI-augmented instruction will focus on technical training specialties with high throughput, complex technical manuals, or heavy digital simulation components,” Hawkins said.

The move follows Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David R. Wolfe’s May announcement calling for the service to build a baseline level of “AI literacy” among all members, as Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.

The document outlines a force-wide push to equip all Airmen with essential AI skills and transform both instruction and personnel management. The command is now drafting a 90-day implementation plan to put the directive’s changes into effect.

“AETC must master the digital domain to build the mission-ready force our Nation requires. This guidance is the roadmap to transform AETC’s infrastructure and data into a cohesive, AI-driven learning ecosystem,” Quinn said in the release.

The command seeks to drive modernized training approaches across the force.

“AETC will lead the Air Force in demonstrating how a large-scale training enterprise can modernize responsibly, fiscally, and at the speed of relevance,” Quinn said.

Larger AI Efforts

The training and education changes come as the service also announced in April that it plans to “aggressively recruit, train, and retain top-tier artificial intelligence professionals.”

While the Air Force is looking to lean on AI to improve everything from command-and-control and sensor-to-shooter timelines in combat, it also plans to leverage the tools for more administrative purposes too.

AETC’s directive, likely in the works for some time, closely follows the release of a RAND Corporation report in August suggesting the Air Force borrow some tips from civilian technology training for its Airmen, as Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. The report recommended basic AI literacy and other tech tools for Airmen and Guardians as key to the service reaching its long-term goals for both initial training and career-long educational improvement.

The RAND report also recommended the service use a “stackable certificates” model for educating Airmen, breaking up long-form, classroom-based, in-person instruction with mobile and remote options and bite-sized learning opportunities to further an Airman’s education.

The “just-in-time” training model recommended by RAND is common across much of civilian tech education curricula.

Implementing New Learning

AETC’s blueprint appears to implement some of the same ideas, like reduced classroom time, more mobile learning, and better scheduling. Initiatives include:

Upgraded WiFi and Networks : Modernizing base network infrastructures to deliver fast, reliable, and secure connectivity that supports heavy virtual learning demands.

Mobile Learning : Expanding secure mobile device access so Airmen can study, train, and complete coursework on the go.

Cutting Classroom Time : Utilizing personalized, AI-augmented learning pathways to reduce the average time-to-train for technical specialties by 20 percent.

Smarter Scheduling : Implementing intelligent scheduling algorithms to optimize flightlines, increase pilot production, and eliminate administrative bottlenecks.

The command is rolling out infrastructure, high-bandwidth and mobile device management upgrades with network modernization and wireless access point expansions across primary training campuses over the next two to three years, Hawkins said.

Divesting and Next Steps

To realize these goals, AETC has initiated an “offset-to-modernize” approach, targeting a 25 percent reduction in legacy software sustainment and overhead by “shutting down redundant, slow, and outdated IT systems,” according to the release.

“We will eliminate duplicative and under-performing capabilities to invest in higher-yield ones that deliver a measurable return in instructional capacity, training throughput, or mission resilience,” Quinn said.

AETC is using an IT Investment Review Board to audit “localized, redundant, and sustainment-intensive legacy software systems across all training wings,” Hawkins said.

“The primary divestment targets are duplicative, on-premises databases and customized legacy applications whose capabilities can be absorbed by modern, enterprise-wide Software-as-a-Service and cloud-native solutions,” Hawkins said.

Command Next Steps (over the next six to 12 months):

Building Enterprise Data Foundations: Establishing a common data layer on the Envision platform, ingesting AETC data sources, and ensuring tier-one mission data is graded as ‘AI-Ready’ based on established quality standards.

Completing 90-Day Implementation Plans: Functional leads (A3/6, A5/8, A9, and the Command Data Office) will complete operational taskings, risk assessments, and granular performance metrics.

Accelerating the IT Investment Review Board: Formalizing command-wide governance to evaluate 100% of new IT spending against cloud-native criteria and begin harvesting legacy sustainment savings.

Foundational Curriculum Integration: Initiating the baseline integration of data and AI literacy standards into Basic Military Training (BMT) and initial technical training doctrine, alongside formalizing Special Experience Identifiers (SEIs) to track Airmen with advanced digital competencies.

Source: AETC

By the end of these efforts, AETC expects to produce “Digital Airmen” through its education and training.

“AETC is integrating basic data and AI literacy standards into 100 percent of its core training pipelines—from Basic Military Training through Professional Military Education,” according to the release. “The command is also formalizing digital skills certifications to help Airmen track, develop, and leverage tech talents throughout their careers.”

items.title: F-16s That Defended Capital on 9/11 Preserved for History
items.author: Tobias Naegele
items.summary: Three F-16s that flew in defense of Washington, D.C., on Sept. 11, 2001, will be retired and preserved as museum artifacts. The post F-16s That Defended Capital on 9/11 Preserved for History appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

Three F-16 s that flew in defense of Washington, D.C., on Sept. 11, 2001, will be retired and preserved as museum artifacts.

The three planes all flew on 9/11: two were among the first three jets to scramble in defense of the capital and the third escorted Air Force One as it returned to Washington later in the day.

On Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist groups hijacked four U.S. airliners, with two striking the twin World Trade Center towers in New York City and the third slamming into the Pentagon near Washington, D.C. The fourth plane was the one that would eventually crash in Shanksville, Pa.

This week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, the National Guard Bureau confirmed that the three planes would be saved:

Tail number 85-1438, flown by now-Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, will go to the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio. His plane was the third to scramble on 9/11.

Tail number 85-1461, flown by now-retired Lt. Gen. Marc Sasseville, will become a static display at Joint Base Andrews. He was the first to scramble, but this was the jet he flew as escort for Air Force One at the end of the day.

Tail number 86-0255, flown by Heather Penney, now director of research at AFA’s Mitchell Institute of Aerospace Studies, will go to the American Heritage Museum in Hudson, Mass. Penney’s was the second plane to scramble, flying with Sasseville.

Saving the Vipers

Members of the wing began research more than a year ago to figure what had happened to the jets flown on that fateful day, tracking down old paperwork to figure out who signed out which aircraft and then to discover where those tails were today.

Working with the National Guard Association of the United States, a nonprofit association that advocates for the Guard, they reached out to the Air Force, the Air National Guard, the White House, and others, offering ideas for preserving the historic aircraft under the National Museum of the United States Air Force Heritage Program.

Among the D.C. National Guard F-16s flown on 9/11, one remains in regular flying status with the Air National Guard’s 162nd Wing in Tucson, Ariz. That was the plane Caine flew, which will eventually go to the Air Force Museum.

Guard advocates learned three other planes flown on 9/11 had been converted into QF-16 Full-Scale Aerial Target drones. One—the jet Sasseville scrambled in—was destroyed at the end of its flying life in a missile test. The remaining two were headed for a similar fate when the issue of saving the planes was raised with the Air Force and others.

Jon “Ice” Eisberg, vice president at NGAUS, said once the issues were clear, the challenge was getting the attention of the right people.

“This was a team effort,” Eisberg said. “We just reached out to some of our normal contacts. We went to the National Security Council. We went to Office of Public Liaison in the White House. We went to the Pentagon, and we alerted some folks up on Capitol Hill to this issue.”

The challenge in saving the planes was that QF-16s are a limited resource. The conversions are expensive, about $5 million apiece. The last of 127 conversions was delivered to the Air Force by contractor Boeing in April 2025, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine’s 2026 USAF & USSF Almanac .

QF-16 drones are used for targeting, and once their available flying hours are used up, they can be used in destructive live ordnance tests. One program that would benefit from such tests is the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, which the Air Force is developing to extend the range of air-to-air combat capabilities beyond visual range.

Still, saving the planes was a priority, and the Air Force came up with a solution: Run down the clock on the QF-16s available flying time, and when their flying hours were all used up, transfer the planes for preservation.

The 9/11 Mission

In a National Guard Bureau video created for the 25th anniversary, Caine recounted his 9/11 experience. “I was running our flying program” that day, Caine recalled. When he saw the second plane hit the World Trade Center on TV, “it was clear that the United States was at war.”

Caine, a major and the wing’s weapons officer at the time, called for live weapons to be readied on the flightline, but getting weapons ready takes time. Soon after, the White House called, he said, “telling us to get airborne.”

Joining Sasseville, a major and the wing’s operations director, and two junior pilots, Penney and Brandon “Igor” Rasmussen, Caine said the group formulated “a hasty, quickly constructed gameplan.”

The clock was ticking as they waited for official authority to launch, and once they had that, weapons were still not ready. Sasseville, who would eventually rise to become Vice Chief of the National Guard Bureau, told Penney as they headed to their plane that they would have to ram the airliner.

“We had an entire wing of support behind us, getting things moving that day, reacting to that terrible attack,” he said. “The White House communicated with us because we were one of the few units in a position to actually do something. … We took off as soon as we could.”

Penney, a young lieutenant and the daughter of an experienced fighter pilot, has wondered why she got the nod that day. “I like to think it was because I was a good pilot,” she said in a recent conversation. “But I think it was because I was single. It was just me and a dog.”

Everyone was operating on adrenaline, Sassevile said. “No one asked any questions.”

Once on the flightline, they dispensed with the routine pilot’s precheck, climbing directly into their planes, trusting their maintainers to have gotten everything ready. Penney had never scrambled an aircraft before—or even trained to.

They took off without clear rules of engagement—these were arranged once they were airborne—and headed out in search of what would later become known as Flight 93, which crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pa., after the passengers stormed the cockpit to stop the terrorists inside.

In fact, they had already done so when Sasseville and Penney took off, but no one knew that at the time.

“We understood what the threat was,” Penney said, recalling their flight up the Potomac River to the northwest of Andrews. “We were looking for a rogue airliner, flying low. We knew they had turned off their transponders.”

Without missiles or bullets—the F-16 has a gun, but they were loaded only with training rounds—the objective target would have to come down with brute force.

“Our only choice,” Penney said, “was going to be to ram the airliner.”

But first they’d have to find it. Unsure of its location or even what vector it was taking to the capital, they headed up the Potomac, then circled back to defend the city. The plan, Sasseville told Penney, was that he would aim his jet at the cockpit and the terrorists, and Penney would take aim at the tail.

The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered all planes in U.S. airspacer to land, and it gradually became clear that Flight 93 had crashed short of the terrorists’ intended target.

Returning to Andrews, Penney recalled looking down at a base that had come alive, its parking lots full, and a line of cars backed up waiting to get on base. “Guardsman came to their units without needing orders, without waiting for paperwork,” she said. They got planes ready, set up cots in the operations area, brought in food. The Guardsman would fly air combat patrols over Washington for the next 90 days straight, and they were already on duty—before they’d ever received orders or even a call.

“They just told their employers, ‘You know, boss, my nation’s calling,’ and they went.”

Now their planes will endure as a reminder of that day and the clear sense of duty those Airmen displayed when the United States came under attack.
